tagline: Administer Azure: identity, governance, storage, compute, networking, and monitoring.

domains.name: Manage Azure identities and governance
domains.description: Manage Microsoft Entra users and groups, assign RBAC roles at the right scope, apply Azure Policy and resource locks, organize resources with tags, management groups and subscriptions, and control spend with budgets, cost alerts, and Advisor.

domains.name: Implement and manage storage
domains.description: Create and secure storage accounts, choose redundancy (LRS/ZRS/GRS), generate SAS tokens and rotate access keys, configure Azure Files and blob containers, manage access tiers, lifecycle policies, soft delete and versioning, and move data with AzCopy and Storage Explorer.

domains.name: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
domains.description: Deploy resources with ARM templates and Bicep, create and resize VMs, attach and manage disks, design for availability with availability sets and zones, scale with VM Scale Sets, and run containers and web apps using Container Registry, Container Instances, Container Apps, and App Service plans with slots, TLS, and custom domains.

domains.name: Implement and manage virtual networking
domains.description: Design VNets and subnets, connect networks with peering, manage public IPs and user-defined routes, filter traffic with NSGs and application security groups, secure access with Azure Bastion, service endpoints and private endpoints, resolve names with Azure DNS, and distribute traffic with Azure Load Balancer.

domains.name: Monitor and maintain Azure resources
domains.description: Use Azure Monitor metrics, logs, alerts and action groups, diagnose connectivity with Network Watcher, and protect workloads with Recovery Services vault, Azure Backup, and Azure Site Recovery failover.

questions.stem: A new contractor needs to start, restart, and resize virtual machines in a single resource group named RG-Web, but must not be able to create or delete any resources or change access for others. Which built-in role assigned at the RG-Web scope best follows least privilege?

options.text: Owner
Contributor
Virtual Machine Contributor
Reader

questions.explanation:
**Correct (C):** Virtual Machine Contributor lets a user manage VMs — start, restart, resize, and configure them — but it does not grant the ability to manage the virtual network or storage, and critically it does not grant access to manage role assignments. Scoping it to RG-Web confines the contractor to that resource group.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **A** Owner grants full control including the ability to grant others access, far more than needed.
- **B** Contributor can create and delete any resource in the scope, violating the no-create/no-delete requirement.
- **D** Reader can only view resources; it cannot start, restart, or resize a VM.
references: AZ-104: Manage Azure identities and governance — Azure RBAC roles and scope

questions.stem: Your organization requires that no virtual machine in the Production subscription can be created in any region outside East US and West US. You must enforce this automatically for all current and future resource groups. What should you implement?

options.text: A CanNotDelete resource lock on the subscription
An Azure Policy assignment using the 'Allowed locations' policy at the subscription scope
A Contributor role assignment limited to East US and West US
A tag named 'region' applied to every resource group

questions.explanation:
**Correct (B):** The built-in 'Allowed locations' Azure Policy with a deny effect prevents resources from being deployed to any region not in the allowed list. Assigning it at the subscription scope makes it apply to every existing and future resource group automatically.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **A** A CanNotDelete lock only blocks deletion; it does nothing to restrict deployment region.
- **C** RBAC roles grant or deny *actions* (such as creating a VM) but cannot restrict the *region* a resource is created in; there is no per-region scoping for roles.
- **D** Tags are metadata for organization and billing; on their own they enforce nothing.
references: AZ-104: Manage Azure identities and governance — Azure Policy

questions.stem: You created a dynamic membership group in Microsoft Entra ID so that any user whose department attribute equals 'Sales' is automatically added. A new hire's department is set to 'Sales', but after several minutes they are still not a member. The rule syntax is valid. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: Dynamic groups only support device membership, not user membership
Dynamic group membership is evaluated and applied automatically by Entra ID, but processing can take time and requires the appropriate licensing; you cannot also add members manually
You must run a PowerShell cmdlet to manually trigger evaluation each time an attribute changes
Dynamic membership rules cannot reference the department attribute

questions.explanation:
**Correct (B):** Dynamic group membership is recalculated automatically by Entra ID whenever relevant attributes change, but the update is not instantaneous — it can take some time to propagate, and dynamic groups require Entra ID P1 (or equivalent) licensing. Membership is owned by the rule, so you cannot manually add or remove members from a dynamic group.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **A** Dynamic groups support both user and device membership; user attributes such as department are commonly used.
- **C** There is no manual trigger cmdlet that admins run per change; evaluation is automatic and continuous.
- **D** The department attribute is a standard, supported attribute for dynamic membership rules.
references: AZ-104: Manage Azure identities and governance — Microsoft Entra groups

questions.stem: You manage governance across many subscriptions using a management group hierarchy. Which statements about management groups are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: An Azure Policy or RBAC assignment made at a management group is inherited by all subscriptions and resources beneath it
A subscription can be a child of only one management group at a time
There is a single root management group that is the ancestor of all other management groups and subscriptions in the directory
Management groups are billed as a separate Azure resource per group
A management group can contain only subscriptions, never other management groups

questions.explanation:
**Correct (A, B, C):** Policy and RBAC assignments at a management group flow down to every child subscription and resource (A). Each subscription has exactly one parent management group (B). Every directory has one tenant root management group at the top of the hierarchy (C).

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **D** Management groups are a free governance container; they are not billed per group.
- **E** Management groups can be nested — a management group can contain both subscriptions and other management groups (up to the supported depth).
references: AZ-104: Manage Azure identities and governance — management groups and subscriptions

questions.stem: A production storage account holds critical data. You apply a ReadOnly lock to it. A few days later an administrator with the Contributor role reports that they can no longer rotate (regenerate) the storage account access keys. Why does the lock block this operation?

options.text: A ReadOnly lock revokes the Contributor role from all users
Regenerating access keys is a write (POST) operation against the account's keys, and a ReadOnly lock blocks all write/modify operations, so key rotation is denied
Access keys can only be rotated by the subscription Owner regardless of locks
A CanNotDelete lock was actually applied, and it blocks key reads

questions.explanation:
**Correct (B):** Listing or regenerating storage account keys is implemented as a write/POST action against the keys, which Azure classifies as a modify operation. A ReadOnly lock permits read operations but blocks every write or modify operation, so it denies key rotation even for a Contributor. This is a well-known gotcha: apply CanNotDelete (not ReadOnly) when you still need to rotate keys.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **A** Locks do not change or remove RBAC role assignments; the administrator still holds Contributor — the lock independently blocks the write.
- **C** Any principal with the right data/management action can rotate keys; rotation is not restricted to the subscription Owner, and a lock would block them too.
- **D** The scenario applied a ReadOnly lock; furthermore a CanNotDelete lock would NOT block key operations, since it only prevents deletion.
references: AZ-104: Manage Azure identities and governance — resource locks

questions.stem: Finance wants to be notified by email as soon as the current month's spending on the Dev subscription reaches 80% of an allotted amount, and again at 100%. Which Cost Management feature should you configure?

options.text: An Azure Monitor metric alert on the subscription
A budget with cost alert thresholds at 80% and 100%
A resource lock that prevents spending above the amount
An Azure Advisor cost recommendation

questions.explanation:
**Correct (B):** A budget in Cost Management lets you set a monetary amount and define alert thresholds (for example 80% and 100%). When actual or forecast spend crosses a threshold, email notifications are sent to the configured recipients.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **A** Azure Monitor metric alerts watch resource performance/usage metrics, not accumulated subscription cost; cost is tracked in Cost Management.
- **C** A resource lock controls delete/modify operations; it cannot cap or monitor spend.
- **D** Advisor gives cost-optimization recommendations but does not alert on reaching a spend threshold.
references: AZ-104: Manage Azure identities and governance — cost management, budgets, and alerts

questions.stem: A user is assigned the Reader role at a resource group and, separately, the Contributor role at one specific storage account inside that resource group. No deny assignment is in play. What effective permissions does the user have on that storage account?

options.text: Reader only, because the resource-group assignment overrides the more specific one
Contributor, because Azure RBAC is additive and the user gets the union of all assignments that apply to the storage account
No access, because conflicting role assignments cancel each other out
Owner, because two roles combine into the next-highest role

questions.explanation:
**Correct (B):** Azure RBAC is additive — a user's effective permissions on a resource are the union of every role assignment that applies to it. The Contributor assignment at the storage account plus the inherited Reader both apply, and the union grants Contributor-level access on that account.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **A** More specific assignments do not override broader ones; permissions accumulate rather than replace.
- **C** Multiple non-deny role assignments do not cancel out; only an explicit deny assignment can subtract permissions.
- **D** Roles do not 'add up' into a higher role; you simply get the combined set of allowed actions, which here equals Contributor.
references: AZ-104: Manage Azure identities and governance — interpret access (effective permissions)

questions.stem: You want to use resource tags to support chargeback and cleanup automation across a subscription. Which statements about Azure tags are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Tags applied to a resource group are automatically inherited by the resources inside it
You can use Azure Policy to require that a specific tag exists on resources, and to append a default tag value when one is missing
Cost Management can group and filter costs by tag for chargeback reporting
A single resource can have many tags, each a name/value pair
Tags are encrypted and never visible to read-only users

questions.explanation:
**Correct (B, C, D):** Azure Policy can enforce required tags and use the 'modify' or 'append' effect to add a default tag value (B). Cost Management lets you slice costs by tag, which is the basis of chargeback (C). Each resource supports many name/value tag pairs (D).

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **A** Tags are NOT automatically inherited; a resource does not get its resource group's tags unless you copy them (commonly via an 'Inherit a tag' policy). This is a frequent exam trap.
- **E** Tags are plain metadata visible to anyone with read access; they are not encrypted and should never hold secrets.
references: AZ-104: Manage Azure identities and governance — tags

questions.stem: You need to grant a colleague the ability to assign roles to other users on a single resource group, but they must NOT be able to deploy, modify, or delete any resources there. Which built-in role should you assign at the resource group scope?

options.text: Owner
Contributor
User Access Administrator
Management Group Contributor

questions.explanation:
**Correct (C):** User Access Administrator grants the ability to manage user access to Azure resources — that is, to create and manage role assignments — without granting any rights to manage the resources themselves. Scoped to the resource group, it lets the colleague delegate access there only.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **A** Owner can both manage access and fully manage resources, which violates the no-deploy/no-modify requirement.
- **B** Contributor can deploy and manage resources but cannot manage role assignments — the exact opposite of what is needed.
- **D** Management Group Contributor manages management groups, not access within a resource group.
references: AZ-104: Manage Azure identities and governance — RBAC and delegation

questions.stem: A storage account must remain readable from applications even if an entire Azure region's primary datacenter becomes unavailable, while also keeping a copy in a secondary region. Cost should be minimized while still meeting this requirement. Which redundancy option should you choose?

options.text: Locally redundant storage (LRS)
Zone-redundant storage (ZRS)
Geo-redundant storage (GRS)
Read-access geo-redundant storage (RA-GRS)

questions.explanation:
**Correct (D):** RA-GRS replicates data to a secondary region AND provides read access to that secondary copy at all times, so applications can keep reading even if the primary region is down. This directly meets the 'readable during a regional outage' requirement.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **C** Plain GRS keeps a secondary-region copy but does NOT allow read access to it unless Microsoft initiates a failover, so apps cannot read during an outage without a failover.
- **B** ZRS protects against datacenter (zone) failure within one region but keeps no copy in a second region.
- **A** LRS keeps three copies in a single datacenter only — no protection against a datacenter or regional outage.
references: AZ-104: Implement and manage storage — storage redundancy

questions.stem: An external partner needs temporary read-only access to a single blob container for 7 days, without being given an Azure account or the storage account keys. You also want to be able to revoke the access early if needed. What should you provide?

options.text: The storage account access key (key1)
A SAS scoped to the container with read permission and an expiry — for example, a service SAS tied to a stored access policy so the access can be revoked early
A Contributor role assignment on the storage account
The storage account connection string

questions.explanation:
**Correct (B):** A shared access signature (SAS) grants scoped, time-limited access to specific resources without exposing account keys or requiring an Azure identity. Limiting it to read on the container with a 7-day expiry meets the requirement, and associating it with a stored access policy lets you revoke it before expiry by deleting/modifying the policy.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **A** The account key grants full control of the entire account and cannot be scoped or easily revoked without rotating the key (which breaks everything using it).
- **C** A Contributor role assignment requires the partner to have an Azure AD identity and grants far broader, write-capable access.
- **D** A connection string contains the account key, so it has the same problems as option A.
references: AZ-104: Implement and manage storage — shared access signatures

questions.stem: You must store compliance logs that are written once and then accessed only a few times a year, but they must remain immediately retrievable when needed. You want the lowest storage cost for a blob that stays online. Which blob access tier is most appropriate?

options.text: Hot
Cool
Archive
Premium

questions.explanation:
**Correct (B):** The Cool tier is designed for infrequently accessed data that must remain online and immediately available. It offers lower storage costs than Hot in exchange for higher access costs, which fits data read only a few times a year.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **A** Hot is optimized for frequently accessed data and has the highest storage cost, more than needed here.
- **C** Archive is the cheapest to store but is offline; retrieving a blob requires a rehydration that can take hours, so it is not 'immediately retrievable'.
- **D** Premium block blob storage targets high-transaction, low-latency workloads and is the most expensive — the opposite of the cost goal.
references: AZ-104: Implement and manage storage — blob access tiers

questions.stem: You want to protect blob data against accidental overwrites and deletions in a general-purpose v2 storage account. Which features help with this goal? Select all that apply.

options.text: Blob soft delete, which retains deleted blobs for a configurable retention period
Blob versioning, which automatically keeps previous versions of a blob when it is overwritten
Container soft delete, which can restore a deleted container within the retention period
Changing the account redundancy from LRS to GRS
Increasing the blob access tier from Cool to Hot

questions.explanation:
**Correct (A, B, C):** Soft delete for blobs retains deleted blobs so they can be recovered (A). Versioning preserves the prior state of a blob whenever it is overwritten or deleted (B). Container soft delete restores an accidentally deleted container within its retention window (C). Together these guard against accidental data loss.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **D** GRS protects against a regional outage by replicating to another region; it does not undo an accidental overwrite or delete — the change is simply replicated.
- **E** Access tier affects cost and retrieval characteristics, not data protection.
references: AZ-104: Implement and manage storage — soft delete and versioning

questions.stem: Several Windows servers need a shared network drive that can be mapped with a drive letter over SMB and is fully managed by Azure. Which storage service should you use?

options.text: Azure Blob storage (block blobs)
Azure Files
Azure Table storage
Azure Queue storage

questions.explanation:
**Correct (B):** Azure Files provides fully managed file shares accessible over the SMB protocol, so Windows clients can mount a share and map it to a drive letter just like a traditional file server.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **A** Blob storage is object storage accessed over HTTP/REST; it is not mounted as an SMB drive letter (Blob's NFS/HNS options are for big-data, not classic drive mapping).
- **C** Table storage is a NoSQL key/attribute store, not a file share.
- **D** Queue storage holds messages for asynchronous communication, not files.
references: AZ-104: Implement and manage storage — Azure Files

questions.stem: You must automatically move blobs in the 'logs' container to the Archive tier once they have not been modified for 90 days, and delete them after 365 days, with no ongoing manual effort. What should you configure?

options.text: A lifecycle management policy on the storage account with rules based on days since last modification
A daily AzCopy script run from an administrator's laptop
Object replication to a second storage account
A stored access policy on the container

questions.explanation:
**Correct (A):** Blob lifecycle management lets you define rules that tier-down (for example to Archive) or delete blobs based on conditions such as days since last modification. The platform evaluates and applies the rules automatically, requiring no ongoing manual work.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **B** A laptop script is manual, fragile, and not the platform-native automated solution the scenario requires.
- **C** Object replication copies blobs to another account; it neither changes tiers nor deletes data on a schedule.
- **D** A stored access policy governs SAS tokens; it has nothing to do with tiering or expiring blobs.
references: AZ-104: Implement and manage storage — lifecycle management

questions.stem: You need to copy several terabytes of data from an on-premises file server to an Azure Blob container as part of a scripted, repeatable migration job that maximizes throughput and supports resuming interrupted transfers. Which tool is the best fit?

options.text: AzCopy command-line utility
Azure Storage Explorer drag-and-drop in the GUI
The Azure portal upload blade
Azure File Sync

questions.explanation:
**Correct (A):** AzCopy is a high-performance command-line tool purpose-built for bulk data transfer to and from Azure Storage. It is scriptable, optimized for throughput, and can resume interrupted jobs — ideal for a repeatable multi-terabyte migration.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **B** Storage Explorer is a graphical tool (it actually uses AzCopy under the hood for large transfers) but its drag-and-drop GUI is not a scripted, automatable job.
- **C** The portal upload blade is meant for small, occasional uploads, not terabyte-scale scripted migration.
- **D** Azure File Sync synchronizes Azure Files shares with Windows servers; it is not a one-time blob migration tool.
references: AZ-104: Implement and manage storage — AzCopy and Storage Explorer

questions.stem: You run a three-tier application across virtual machines in a single Azure region. The business requires that the application stay available even if an entire datacenter (one physical location in the region) fails. Which approach meets this requirement?

options.text: Place all VMs in a single availability set
Use a proximity placement group
Distribute the VMs across multiple availability zones in the region
Enable accelerated networking on each VM

questions.explanation:
**Correct (C):** Availability zones are physically separate datacenters within a region, each with independent power, cooling, and networking. Spreading VMs across zones keeps the application running even if one entire datacenter (zone) fails, which is exactly the stated requirement.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **A** An availability set protects against failures within a single datacenter (rack/host/update domain level), not the loss of an entire datacenter.
- **B** A proximity placement group keeps VMs physically close to reduce latency — the opposite of spreading them across datacenters for resilience.
- **D** Accelerated networking improves network performance; it provides no datacenter-level fault tolerance.
references: AZ-104: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources — availability zones and sets

questions.stem: A web app hosted in Azure App Service must let you test a new release on a staging URL and then switch it into production with no downtime, keeping the ability to roll back instantly. Which App Service feature delivers this?

options.text: Scaling out the App Service plan
Always On
A custom domain binding
Deployment slots with a swap operation

questions.explanation:
**Correct (D):** Deployment slots let you deploy a new build to a staging slot with its own URL, validate it, then swap it into the production slot. The swap exchanges the slots without downtime, and because the previous production content is now in the staging slot, you can swap back instantly to roll back.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **A** Scaling out adds instances for capacity; it does nothing for staged releases or zero-downtime swaps.
- **C** A custom domain binding maps a domain name to the app; it is unrelated to staged deployments.
- **B** Always On keeps the app warm so it is not unloaded when idle; it does not provide staging or swap.
references: AZ-104: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources — App Service deployment slots

questions.stem: You manage a VM Scale Set that hosts a stateless web tier. You want it to add instances automatically when average CPU across the set stays above 70% and remove instances when it drops below 30%, within a defined min/max count. What should you configure?

options.text: Autoscale rules based on the CPU metric with scale-out and scale-in thresholds and instance limits
A larger VM SKU for each instance
An availability set around the scale set
A load balancer health probe

questions.explanation:
**Correct (A):** VM Scale Sets support autoscale rules that watch a metric such as average CPU and add or remove instances when thresholds are crossed, bounded by a configured minimum and maximum. This matches the scale-out at 70% / scale-in at 30% requirement exactly.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **B** Choosing a larger SKU is vertical scaling and is fixed; it does not automatically adjust instance count to load.
- **C** An availability set affects fault/update domains for resiliency, not automatic scaling.
- **D** A health probe checks instance health for load balancing; it does not trigger scaling based on CPU.
references: AZ-104: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources — VM Scale Sets autoscale

questions.stem: A developer wants to run a single short-lived containerized batch job from an image in Azure Container Registry. It should start quickly, bill per second while running, and require no cluster or VM management. Which Azure service best fits?

options.text: Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS)
An App Service plan in the Premium tier
Azure Container Instances (ACI)
A dedicated VM running Docker

questions.explanation:
**Correct (C):** Azure Container Instances runs individual containers on demand with per-second billing and no orchestrator, node pool, or VM to manage. It is the simplest way to run a short, single-purpose containerized job.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **A** AKS is a managed Kubernetes cluster intended for orchestrating many long-running containers; it is heavyweight for one short job and you still manage node pools.
- **B** An App Service plan reserves compute for web hosting and is not optimized for one-off per-second container jobs.
- **D** A dedicated VM requires you to manage the OS and Docker yourself and bills for the whole VM, not per second of the job.
references: AZ-104: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources — Azure Container Instances

questions.stem: Arrange the following high-level steps in the correct order to deploy an Azure resource using a Bicep file from your workstation. (Place the steps in sequence.)

options.text: Author the Bicep file describing the resources
Sign in with the Azure CLI and select the target subscription
Run 'az deployment group create' referencing the Bicep file and a target resource group
Verify the deployed resources in the Azure portal or with the CLI

questions.explanation:
**Correct order (A, B, C, D):** First author the Bicep file that declares the desired resources (A). Next authenticate and set context by signing in with the Azure CLI and selecting the subscription (B). Then submit the deployment with 'az deployment group create', pointing at the Bicep file and the target resource group (C). Finally confirm the resources were created as expected by checking the portal or querying with the CLI (D).

A common mistake is to attempt the deployment before signing in/selecting the subscription, which fails authentication, or to skip the final verification step that confirms the desired state was achieved.
references: AZ-104: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources — ARM templates and Bicep

questions.stem: You must resize an existing Azure VM to a SKU that is not offered on the physical host currently allocated to that VM. The VM is not in an availability set. What is the correct way to make the new size available?

options.text: Delete and recreate the VM from scratch; resizing to an unavailable SKU is impossible
Convert the OS disk from Standard HDD to Premium SSD, which unlocks all SKUs
Add the VM to a proximity placement group and then resize
Stop (deallocate) the VM, then resize it, which lets Azure reallocate it to a host that supports the new size

questions.explanation:
**Correct (D):** If the desired size is not supported on the current host, you must stop (deallocate) the VM first. Deallocation releases the VM from its current host so that, when you resize and restart, Azure can place it on a host cluster that offers the target size.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **A** You do not need to recreate the VM; deallocating and resizing is the supported path.
- **C** Proximity placement groups control physical closeness to reduce latency; they do not expand which SKUs a host can offer (they can actually make placement harder).
- **B** Disk type affects performance and which VM families support premium storage, but changing the disk does not make every VM size available on the current host.
references: AZ-104: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources — resize virtual machines

questions.stem: You are choosing between Azure managed disk types for various VM roles. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Premium SSD and Ultra Disk are recommended for I/O-intensive, production database workloads
Managed disks handle the underlying storage account, so you do not create or manage one yourself
Standard HDD is the lowest-cost option suited to infrequently accessed, non-critical data
Changing a VM's OS disk to a larger size is impossible once the VM is created
Managed disks cannot be encrypted at rest

questions.explanation:
**Correct (A, B, C):** Premium SSD and Ultra Disk deliver the high IOPS and low latency that production databases need (A). With managed disks Azure manages the storage account behind the scenes, removing that administrative burden (B). Standard HDD is the cheapest tier, appropriate for backup or infrequently accessed data (C).

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **D** You can expand a managed disk to a larger size (typically requiring a stop/restart and a resize of the disk); it is not impossible.
- **E** Managed disks are encrypted at rest by default with platform-managed keys, and can also use customer-managed keys.
references: AZ-104: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources — managed disks

questions.stem: Your team runs an event-driven microservice in containers that must scale to zero when idle and scale out on HTTP traffic, without you managing Kubernetes infrastructure. Which Azure service is designed for this?

options.text: Azure Container Apps
Azure Virtual Machine Scale Sets
Azure Container Registry
Azure Batch

questions.explanation:
**Correct (A):** Azure Container Apps is a serverless container platform built on Kubernetes and KEDA that supports event- and HTTP-driven autoscaling, including scaling to zero when there is no traffic, all without you managing the underlying cluster.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **B** VM Scale Sets autoscale VMs, not serverless containers, and they cannot scale to zero instances while staying ready to serve HTTP without extra plumbing.
- **C** Azure Container Registry stores and manages container images; it does not run or scale containers.
- **D** Azure Batch runs large-scale parallel batch compute jobs, not always-on HTTP microservices that scale to zero.
references: AZ-104: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources — Azure Container Apps

questions.stem: You are about to deploy two web apps and one API app that should all share the same underlying compute and scaling configuration to control cost. In App Service, what determines the compute resources, pricing tier, and scaling for the apps?

options.text: The App Service plan
The deployment slot
The custom domain
The TLS/SSL binding

questions.explanation:
**Correct (A):** The App Service plan defines the region, the underlying VM size/SKU, the pricing tier, and the scaling settings. Multiple apps placed in the same plan share that compute, which is how you consolidate cost.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **B** A deployment slot is a separate environment for staging/swapping within an app; it does not define the plan's compute or pricing.
- **C** A custom domain maps a hostname to an app; it has no bearing on compute or scaling.
- **D** A TLS/SSL binding secures traffic for a hostname; it does not determine compute resources or tier.
references: AZ-104: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources — App Service plans

questions.stem: Two virtual networks, VNet-A (East US) and VNet-B (West US), each host VMs that must communicate privately by their private IP addresses with low latency and without traversing the public internet. Neither network uses overlapping address spaces. What is the simplest way to connect them?

options.text: Configure a site-to-site VPN gateway between them
Assign public IP addresses to all VMs and allow traffic in the NSGs
Configure global VNet peering between VNet-A and VNet-B
Deploy Azure Bastion in each VNet

questions.explanation:
**Correct (C):** VNet peering connects two virtual networks over the Microsoft backbone so resources communicate using private IPs with low latency and no public-internet exposure. Because the VNets are in different regions, you use global VNet peering. It is simpler than a gateway because no VPN devices or tunnels are involved.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **A** A VPN gateway works but adds gateways, tunnels, and overhead and routes over encrypted tunnels; peering is the simpler, lower-latency choice for Azure-to-Azure connectivity.
- **B** Public IPs send traffic over the internet, violating the 'private, not over the public internet' requirement.
- **D** Azure Bastion provides secure RDP/SSH from the portal to VMs; it does not interconnect two VNets for general traffic.
references: AZ-104: Implement and manage virtual networking — VNet peering

questions.stem: A subnet has an NSG that allows inbound TCP 443 from the internet. The network interface of a VM in that subnet has its own NSG that denies inbound TCP 443. Inbound HTTPS traffic from the internet arrives at the VM. What happens?

options.text: The traffic is allowed because the subnet NSG takes priority over the NIC NSG
An error occurs because a subnet and a NIC cannot both have an NSG
The traffic is allowed because at least one NSG allows it
The traffic is denied because, for inbound traffic, both the subnet NSG and the NIC NSG are evaluated and the NIC NSG blocks it

questions.explanation:
**Correct (D):** For inbound traffic to a VM, Azure evaluates the subnet NSG first and then the NIC NSG; the traffic must be allowed by BOTH to reach the VM. Since the NIC NSG denies 443, the HTTPS traffic is dropped even though the subnet NSG allows it.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **A** Neither NSG 'takes priority' over the other; both must allow the flow. A deny at either layer wins.
- **C** NSGs are not 'allow if any'; an allow in one does not override a deny in the other for that direction.
- **B** A subnet and a NIC can each have their own NSG simultaneously; this is fully supported and both apply.
references: AZ-104: Implement and manage virtual networking — network security groups

questions.stem: You must let administrators connect to VMs via RDP and SSH through the Azure portal without exposing any public IP addresses or RDP/SSH ports on the VMs to the internet. Which service provides this?

options.text: Azure Bastion deployed in the virtual network
A public load balancer with inbound NAT rules
A user-defined route forcing traffic to a firewall
A service endpoint to Microsoft.Compute

questions.explanation:
**Correct (A):** Azure Bastion is a managed PaaS service deployed into a VNet that provides secure RDP and SSH connectivity to VMs directly from the Azure portal over TLS. The VMs need no public IP and you do not open RDP/SSH ports to the internet.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **B** A public load balancer with NAT rules requires a public IP and exposed ports — exactly what must be avoided.
- **C** A user-defined route changes traffic paths but does not provide browser-based RDP/SSH or remove the need for public exposure.
- **D** Service endpoints secure access to Azure PaaS services over the backbone; they do not provide RDP/SSH connectivity to VMs.
references: AZ-104: Implement and manage virtual networking — Azure Bastion

questions.stem: Traffic leaving a subnet must be forced through a network virtual appliance (firewall) at 10.0.1.4 instead of using Azure's default routing. What should you create and associate with the subnet?

options.text: A network security group rule allowing all outbound traffic
A public IP address on the firewall
A route table containing a user-defined route with next hop type 'Virtual appliance' set to 10.0.1.4, associated with the subnet
A service endpoint policy

questions.explanation:
**Correct (C):** To override Azure's system routes you create a route table with a user-defined route (UDR) whose next hop type is 'Virtual appliance' and whose next hop address is the NVA (10.0.1.4), then associate the route table with the subnet. Traffic from the subnet is then steered to the firewall.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **A** An NSG filters (allows/denies) traffic; it cannot redirect traffic to a specific next hop.
- **B** A public IP on the firewall does not change how subnet traffic is routed internally.
- **D** A service endpoint policy restricts which storage/PaaS resources can be reached over a service endpoint; it does not redirect general egress to an appliance.
references: AZ-104: Implement and manage virtual networking — user-defined routes

questions.stem: You must ensure that an Azure SQL Database is reachable only over a private IP inside your virtual network and not via its public endpoint, so traffic never traverses the public internet. Which feature should you implement?

options.text: A service endpoint for Microsoft.Sql on the subnet
A public IP with a firewall rule for the VNet
A network security group blocking outbound internet
A private endpoint for the Azure SQL Database with public network access disabled

questions.explanation:
**Correct (D):** A private endpoint projects the Azure SQL resource into your VNet with a private IP address from your subnet, and disabling public network access ensures the database is reachable only over that private connection. Traffic stays on the Microsoft backbone and never uses the public endpoint.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **A** A service endpoint secures the PaaS service to the subnet but the service is still accessed via its public IP/endpoint over the backbone; it does not give the resource a private IP inside your VNet, so it does not meet 'reachable only over a private IP'.
- **C** Blocking outbound internet in an NSG does not change how the SQL service is published or give it a private IP.
- **B** Using a public IP/firewall rule still exposes the public endpoint, the opposite of the requirement.
references: AZ-104: Implement and manage virtual networking — private endpoints vs service endpoints

questions.stem: You must distribute inbound TCP traffic from the internet across three VMs in the same region for a non-HTTP, latency-sensitive game server, operating at the transport layer (Layer 4). Which Azure service is the best fit?

options.text: A public Azure Load Balancer
Azure Application Gateway
Azure Front Door
Azure Traffic Manager

questions.explanation:
**Correct (A):** Azure Load Balancer is a Layer 4 (TCP/UDP) load balancer. A public Load Balancer can distribute inbound internet traffic across a backend pool of VMs in a region with low latency, which suits a non-HTTP transport-layer workload like a game server.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **B** Application Gateway is a Layer 7 (HTTP/HTTPS) load balancer with URL-based routing; it is for web traffic, not arbitrary TCP/UDP.
- **C** Azure Front Door is a global Layer 7 application delivery/CDN service for HTTP(S), not a regional Layer 4 balancer.
- **D** Traffic Manager is DNS-based global routing; it directs clients to endpoints by DNS responses and does not proxy TCP traffic at Layer 4.
references: AZ-104: Implement and manage virtual networking — Azure Load Balancer

questions.stem: You want to simplify NSG rule management for a multi-tier app by grouping VM network interfaces logically (for example 'web' and 'db') and writing rules against those groups. Which statements about application security groups (ASGs) are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: An NSG rule can use an ASG as its source or destination instead of explicit IP ranges
You assign a VM's network interface to one or more ASGs to make it a member
ASGs let you group NICs by workload role so rules follow the role rather than fixed IPs
An ASG replaces the need for any NSG
ASGs automatically encrypt traffic between member NICs

questions.explanation:
**Correct (A, B, C):** ASGs can be referenced as the source or destination in NSG rules in place of IP ranges (A). You make a NIC a member by assigning it to one or more ASGs (B). This lets you express rules by workload role, so they keep working as IPs change (C).

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **D** ASGs do not replace NSGs; they are referenced *by* NSG rules. You still need an NSG to allow or deny traffic.
- **E** ASGs are a grouping construct for rule authoring; they do not encrypt traffic.
references: AZ-104: Implement and manage virtual networking — application security groups

questions.stem: You need an alert that fires when a VM's average CPU exceeds 85% for 5 minutes, and the alert must both email the on-call team and trigger an Azure Function for automated remediation. Which combination should you configure in Azure Monitor?

options.text: A metric alert rule on CPU bound to an action group that contains an email and an Azure Function action
A diagnostic setting that streams logs to a storage account
A budget with an alert threshold of 85%
A resource lock that triggers on high CPU

questions.explanation:
**Correct (A):** In Azure Monitor you create a metric alert rule that evaluates the CPU metric against the 85%/5-minute condition. The alert's notifications and automated responses are defined in an action group, which can contain both an email action and an Azure Function action — satisfying both the notify and remediate requirements.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **B** A diagnostic setting only routes telemetry to a destination; it does not evaluate a threshold or send notifications.
- **C** A budget tracks cost, not CPU, and cannot invoke a Function for remediation.
- **D** Resource locks govern delete/modify operations and have no alerting or trigger capability.
references: AZ-104: Monitor and maintain Azure resources — Azure Monitor alerts and action groups

questions.stem: Two VMs in different subnets cannot communicate, and you must determine whether an NSG rule is blocking the traffic and which rule is responsible. Which Network Watcher capability should you use?

options.text: Connection Monitor latency dashboard only
Traffic Analytics billing report
IP flow verify (and/or NSG diagnostics) to test whether a packet would be allowed or denied and identify the matching rule
Packet capture of the storage account

questions.explanation:
**Correct (C):** Network Watcher's IP flow verify checks whether a packet to or from a VM would be allowed or denied based on the effective NSG rules and tells you which specific rule made the decision — exactly what is needed to find the blocking rule.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **A** Connection Monitor measures connectivity and latency over time; it does not pinpoint the specific NSG rule allowing or denying a given flow.
- **B** Traffic Analytics summarizes traffic patterns and is not a billing report, nor does it test a single flow against rules in real time.
- **D** Packet capture records traffic on a VM's NIC, not on a storage account, and is more involved than needed to identify a blocking rule.
references: AZ-104: Monitor and maintain Azure resources — Network Watcher

questions.stem: You must schedule daily backups of several Azure VMs with 30-day retention and centralized restore management, using a native Azure service. Where are these VM backups configured and stored?

options.text: In an Azure Storage account using blob snapshots managed manually
In an Azure Monitor Log Analytics workspace
In Azure Site Recovery replication only
In a Recovery Services vault using Azure Backup with a backup policy

questions.explanation:
**Correct (D):** Azure Backup protects Azure VMs by associating them with a backup policy (schedule and retention) stored in a Recovery Services vault. The vault provides centralized management of recovery points and restores, meeting the daily/30-day requirement natively.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **A** Manual blob snapshots are not a managed backup solution and lack policy-driven scheduling, retention, and centralized restore.
- **C** Azure Site Recovery is for disaster-recovery replication and failover between regions, not scheduled point-in-time backups with retention policies.
- **B** A Log Analytics workspace stores monitoring/log data, not VM backups.
references: AZ-104: Monitor and maintain Azure resources — Recovery Services vault and Azure Backup

questions.stem: You are designing disaster recovery for Azure VMs using Azure Site Recovery (ASR) to a secondary region. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: ASR continuously replicates VM data to the target region so you can fail over with minimal data loss
A recovery plan lets you orchestrate the failover order of multiple VMs and add steps
You can run a test failover to validate DR without affecting the production workload
ASR replaces the need for Azure Backup because it keeps long-term point-in-time backups
Failover is only possible if the primary region is completely destroyed

questions.explanation:
**Correct (A, B, C):** ASR continuously replicates VMs to a secondary region, enabling failover with low RPO (A). Recovery plans orchestrate the sequence in which VMs fail over and can include scripts/manual actions (B). A test failover spins up the workload in an isolated network to validate DR without impacting production (C).

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **D** ASR provides disaster-recovery replication and failover, not long-term point-in-time backups; Azure Backup serves the backup/retention role, so ASR does not replace it.
- **E** You can initiate a planned or unplanned failover at any time (for example for DR drills or partial outages); it is not limited to total destruction of the primary region.
references: AZ-104: Monitor and maintain Azure resources — Azure Site Recovery and failover

questions.stem: A vendor's engineer who already has their own Microsoft Entra account (vendorcorp.com) needs to manage resources in three resource groups in your tenant for the next two months. You must not create or maintain a password for them, and you want to assign Azure RBAC roles to their identity directly. What should you do?

options.text: Create a new cloud-only member user in your tenant and email the temporary password to the engineer
Create a service principal in your tenant and share its client secret with the engineer
Add the engineer's vendorcorp.com account to a security group and assign the group an Microsoft Entra directory role
Invite the engineer as a guest (B2B) user, then assign the appropriate RBAC roles to the guest object on the resource groups

questions.explanation:
**Correct (D):** Microsoft Entra B2B collaboration invites the external person as a guest using their existing home-tenant credentials, so you never manage a password for them. Once the guest object exists in your directory you assign Azure RBAC roles to it at the resource-group scope exactly as you would for any member.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **A** A cloud-only member user forces you to create and manage a password, which the requirement explicitly forbids, and duplicates an identity the engineer already has.
- **C** Microsoft Entra directory roles grant tenant-level administrative permissions, not the scoped resource-group access required; the task calls for Azure RBAC, not a directory role.
- **B** A service principal is a non-human application identity; sharing its secret with a person is a credential-handling anti-pattern and does not represent the engineer's own identity.
references: AZ-104: Manage Azure identities and governance — Microsoft Entra users and guests

questions.stem: An Azure Policy assignment uses the DeployIfNotExists effect to deploy a diagnostic setting on every new storage account. After assignment, existing non-compliant storage accounts are reported as non-compliant but are NOT being remediated automatically. What must you configure so the policy can fix the existing resources?

options.text: Change the policy effect from DeployIfNotExists to Deny so non-compliant accounts are blocked
Create a remediation task for the assignment and ensure its managed identity has the roles listed in the policy's roleDefinitionIds
Add an exemption for each existing storage account so the policy stops reporting them
Re-scope the assignment to a management group so inheritance forces remediation

questions.explanation:
**Correct (B):** DeployIfNotExists only auto-deploys on resource create/update events. To bring already-existing resources into compliance you trigger a remediation task, which runs the embedded deployment using the assignment's managed identity. That identity must hold the roles declared in the policy definition's roleDefinitionIds, or the deployment fails.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **A** Deny prevents future non-compliant accounts but cannot deploy a diagnostic setting onto existing ones, so it does not remediate.
- **C** An exemption merely suppresses the compliance evaluation; it leaves the resources unconfigured rather than fixing them.
- **D** Changing scope does not retroactively run the deployment; remediation of existing resources still requires a remediation task regardless of scope.
references: AZ-104: Manage Azure identities and governance — Azure Policy remediation

questions.stem: You assign the built-in Contributor role to a team at the subscription scope. The team reports they can create and manage resources but cannot grant other users access to those resources. They need to keep creating resources but should never be able to manage access assignments. Which statement correctly explains this behavior?

options.text: Contributor lacks Microsoft.Authorization/*/write, so it cannot create or edit role assignments; this is expected and no change is needed
Contributor is broken at subscription scope and must be reassigned at the resource-group scope to work correctly
You must also assign Reader so Contributor can read and then write role assignments
Contributor can manage access, so a deny assignment from a blueprint is overriding it and must be removed

questions.explanation:
**Correct (A):** The built-in Contributor role grants full management of resources but deliberately excludes Microsoft.Authorization actions for writing role assignments, locks, and policies. The observed behavior is by design and matches the requirement that the team manage resources but not access, so no change is needed.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **B** Role scope does not change which permissions Contributor includes; reassigning at resource-group scope yields the same access-management restriction.
- **C** Reader only adds read permissions and cannot grant the ability to write role assignments.
- **D** Contributor cannot manage access in the first place, so attributing the behavior to a deny assignment is incorrect.
references: AZ-104: Manage Azure identities and governance — Azure RBAC built-in roles

questions.stem: Your company is billed for many subscriptions and wants to apply one Azure Policy that enforces a required 'CostCenter' tag across every current and future subscription, without re-assigning the policy each time a new subscription is created. At which scope should you assign the policy?

options.text: On each individual subscription separately
On a single resource group that all teams share
On the management group that contains the subscriptions
On each resource as it is created

questions.explanation:
**Correct (C):** Assigning the policy at a management group makes it inherit down to every subscription beneath it, including subscriptions added later. This gives one assignment that covers current and future subscriptions automatically.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **A** Per-subscription assignment must be repeated for every new subscription, which the requirement forbids.
- **B** A resource group scope covers only the resources in that group, not whole subscriptions.
- **D** Per-resource assignment is unmanageable and does not provide inheritance for future resources or subscriptions.
references: AZ-104: Manage Azure identities and governance — Azure Policy scope and management groups

questions.stem: You want to control Azure spend on the Dev subscription. Which statements about Microsoft Cost Management budgets are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: A budget can trigger alerts at configurable percentage thresholds of the budgeted amount
A budget alert can invoke an action group to run automation, such as stopping resources
Reaching a cost budget's amount automatically blocks the creation of new resources in the subscription
Budgets can be scoped to a subscription or to a resource group

questions.explanation:
**Correct (A, B, D):** Cost Management budgets fire alerts at percentage thresholds you define (A), can be wired to an action group to trigger automation like stopping VMs (B), and can be scoped at the subscription or resource-group level (D).

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **C** A budget is a notification and automation trigger, not an enforcement gate; reaching the amount does not by itself prevent new resource creation. Blocking deployment requires Azure Policy or RBAC controls.
references: AZ-104: Manage Azure identities and governance — cost management budgets and alerts

questions.stem: A production resource group contains a public IP, a VNet, and several VMs. You must prevent anyone — including subscription Owners — from deleting any resource in this group, while still allowing routine configuration changes such as resizing VMs. What should you apply?

options.text: A ReadOnly lock on the resource group
A CanNotDelete lock on the resource group
An Azure Policy with the Deny effect on delete operations
Remove the Owner role from all users on the resource group

questions.explanation:
**Correct (B):** A CanNotDelete (Delete) lock applied at the resource group blocks deletion of the group and the resources inside it for all principals regardless of their RBAC role, while still permitting read and modify operations such as resizing a VM.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **A** A ReadOnly lock also blocks updates, so VMs could not be resized, violating the requirement to allow configuration changes.
- **C** Azure Policy governs resource properties and create-time conditions; a delete-blocking guardrail is the purpose of a lock, and Policy does not override an Owner's ability to delete the way a lock does.
- **D** Removing Owner reduces who can delete but does not stop remaining Owners or higher scopes, and breaks legitimate administration.
references: AZ-104: Manage Azure identities and governance — resource locks

questions.stem: Your HR system writes each employee's 'jobTitle' attribute into Microsoft Entra ID. You need a group whose membership always reflects every user whose jobTitle equals 'Field Technician', with no manual maintenance as people are hired or change roles. What should you create?

options.text: An assigned security group and add each Field Technician manually
A Microsoft 365 group with an owner who reviews membership monthly
A dynamic membership security group with a rule like (user.jobTitle -eq "Field Technician")
A distribution list synchronized from on-premises Active Directory

questions.explanation:
**Correct (C):** A dynamic membership group evaluates a membership rule against user attributes and automatically adds or removes members as those attributes change, so the group stays accurate as people are hired or reassigned without manual effort. (Dynamic membership requires Microsoft Entra ID P1.)

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **A** An assigned group requires manual additions and removals, exactly what the requirement rules out.
- **B** Owner-driven monthly review is still manual and lags behind attribute changes.
- **D** A synced distribution list does not provide attribute-based dynamic membership for cloud authorization and is for email distribution, not RBAC group logic.
references: AZ-104: Manage Azure identities and governance — dynamic membership groups

questions.stem: A user is granted the Owner role at a management group but is also the target of a deny assignment (created by an Azure Blueprints assignment) that denies Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/delete at a child subscription. The user attempts to delete a storage account in that subscription. What is the result, and why?

options.text: The deletion succeeds because Owner at a higher scope always overrides lower-scope restrictions
The deletion succeeds because deny assignments apply only to guest users
The deletion is blocked because deny assignments take precedence over role assignments
The deletion is blocked only if a CanNotDelete lock also exists

questions.explanation:
**Correct (C):** In the Azure RBAC evaluation model, deny assignments are evaluated before and take precedence over role assignments. Even an Owner is blocked from an action that a deny assignment explicitly denies at the applicable scope, so the storage-account deletion fails.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **A** A higher-scope Owner assignment does not override a deny assignment; precedence runs the other way.
- **B** Deny assignments are not limited to guests; they apply to whatever principals the assignment specifies.
- **D** The deny assignment alone blocks the action; a separate lock is not required for the deny to take effect.
references: AZ-104: Manage Azure identities and governance — Azure RBAC and deny assignments

questions.stem: You must give a support engineer the Virtual Machine Contributor role on a single resource group using the Azure portal. Arrange the steps in the correct order. (Place the steps in sequence.)

options.text: Open the target resource group and select Access control (IAM)
Choose Add > Add role assignment and select the Virtual Machine Contributor role
On the Members tab, select the support engineer as the assigned principal
Review and assign, then confirm the assignment appears under Role assignments

questions.explanation:
**Correct order (A, B, C, D):** Scope the assignment by opening the resource group's Access control (IAM) blade (A). Begin the assignment and pick the role, Virtual Machine Contributor (B). Select the principal who receives the role (C). Finally review and assign, then verify it shows under Role assignments (D).

A frequent mistake is selecting the principal before choosing the role, or assigning at the wrong scope (subscription instead of the resource group), which grants broader access than intended.
references: AZ-104: Manage Azure identities and governance — assign RBAC roles in the portal

questions.stem: You are standardizing resource tagging for cost reporting. Which statements about Azure resource tags are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: A tag applied to a resource group is automatically inherited by the resources inside it for billing
Azure Policy can append or require specific tags on resources at creation time
Tags appear on the detailed usage and cost data, enabling cost grouping by tag
Each resource can have many tags as name/value pairs

questions.explanation:
**Correct (B, C, D):** Azure Policy can use modify/append effects to require or add tags when resources are created (B). Tags surface in detailed billing/usage exports so costs can be grouped and filtered by tag (C). Resources support multiple name/value tag pairs (D).

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **A** Tags are NOT automatically inherited by child resources from a resource group; resources only show the resource group's tags if a policy or process explicitly applies them. This is a classic distractor.
references: AZ-104: Manage Azure identities and governance — resource tags and cost

questions.stem: An application currently uses storage account access key 1 in its connection string. You must rotate keys with zero downtime: regenerate the compromised key without breaking the running application. What is the correct sequence of actions?

options.text: Regenerate key 1 first, then update the app to key 1's new value
Regenerate both keys at the same time, then restart the app
Delete the storage account and recreate it to get fresh keys
Switch the app's connection string to key 2, then regenerate key 1

questions.explanation:
**Correct (D):** A storage account has two keys precisely to allow zero-downtime rotation. First move the application to key 2 so it is no longer using key 1, then regenerate key 1. The app keeps working on key 2 throughout, and key 1 is now safely rotated.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **A** Regenerating key 1 while the app still uses key 1 immediately breaks the running application until the string is updated, causing downtime.
- **C** Recreating the account is destructive and unnecessary, and changes the account identity.
- **B** Regenerating both keys simultaneously invalidates whatever key the app is using, guaranteeing an outage.
references: AZ-104: Implement and manage storage — rotate storage account access keys

questions.stem: You issue a service SAS for a blob container and set its expiry to 30 days. A few hours later you discover the SAS was leaked. You must invalidate the leaked SAS immediately, even though its expiry is far in the future, while issuing replacement SAS tokens for legitimate clients. What should you do?

options.text: Wait until the SAS reaches its expiry time; SAS tokens cannot be revoked early
Change the storage account's network firewall to block the leaker's IP
Regenerate the storage account key that signed the SAS, which invalidates all SAS tokens signed with that key, then reissue tokens
Apply a CanNotDelete lock to the container so the SAS can no longer be used

questions.explanation:
**Correct (C):** A service SAS is signed with a storage account key. Regenerating that key immediately invalidates every SAS signed with it, including the leaked one, regardless of its remaining lifetime. You then reissue new SAS tokens for valid clients. (A stored access policy is the alternative, but with a plain ad-hoc SAS, key regeneration is the way to revoke.)

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **A** SAS can be revoked early — exactly by regenerating the signing key or revoking the stored access policy — so waiting is wrong.
- **B** An IP firewall rule may not match the attacker and does not invalidate the token itself.
- **D** A delete lock prevents resource deletion; it has no effect on SAS validity or data access.
references: AZ-104: Implement and manage storage — SAS tokens and revocation

questions.stem: A storage account in East US must keep three synchronous copies of data in the primary region and additionally replicate asynchronously to a paired secondary region for disaster recovery, with read access to the secondary at all times. Which redundancy option meets this?

options.text: Locally redundant storage (LRS)
Zone-redundant storage (ZRS)
Read-access geo-redundant storage (RA-GRS)
Geo-redundant storage (GRS) without read access

questions.explanation:
**Correct (C):** RA-GRS keeps copies in the primary region and replicates to the paired secondary region, and crucially exposes a read-only endpoint to the secondary that you can read from at any time. That matches the requirement for cross-region DR plus always-available secondary reads.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **A** LRS keeps copies only within a single datacenter and provides no regional DR.
- **B** ZRS spreads copies across availability zones in one region but does not replicate to a second region.
- **D** Plain GRS replicates to the secondary but does not provide read access to it unless a failover occurs.
references: AZ-104: Implement and manage storage — redundancy options

questions.stem: You enabled blob versioning and blob soft delete on a storage account. A process overwrites an important blob with bad data. You need to restore the previous good content with the least effort. What should you do?

options.text: Restore from the most recent Azure Backup recovery point of the storage account
Fail the account over to its secondary region
Recover the deleted container from soft delete
Promote the previous blob version to the current version

questions.explanation:
**Correct (D):** With blob versioning, every overwrite automatically creates a prior version of the blob. To undo a bad overwrite you simply promote (copy) the last good version back to the current (base) blob, which is the least-effort recovery for an overwrite.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **A** A storage-account-level Azure Backup may not be configured and is heavier than promoting an existing version that already exists.
- **C** Container soft delete recovers a deleted container, but here the container and blob still exist — only the content was overwritten, not deleted.
- **B** Account failover is a regional DR action and does not undo a logical overwrite that has already replicated.
references: AZ-104: Implement and manage storage — blob versioning and soft delete

questions.stem: You are designing a lifecycle management policy for a general-purpose v2 storage account to control blob costs. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Lifecycle rules can move blobs to Cool or Archive based on days since last modification
Lifecycle rules can delete blobs (and blob versions) after a specified age
Lifecycle rules can be filtered to specific containers or blob name prefixes
Lifecycle rules apply to the page blobs that back managed disks the same way they apply to block blobs

questions.explanation:
**Correct (A, B, C):** Lifecycle management can tier blobs to Cool or Archive based on age/last-modified or last-access (A), delete blobs and old versions/snapshots after a set age (B), and be scoped with filters on containers and blob name prefixes (C).

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **D** Lifecycle policies target block blobs (and append blobs for delete); the page blobs backing Azure managed disks are managed by the disk resource, not by storage lifecycle tiering, so treating them identically is incorrect.
references: AZ-104: Implement and manage storage — blob lifecycle management

questions.stem: A data blob is in the Archive access tier. A team now needs to read it within the next several hours. What must happen before the data can be read, and how do you initiate it?

options.text: Nothing special; archived blobs can be read directly like Hot or Cool blobs
You must rehydrate the blob by changing its tier to Hot or Cool (or copying it to an online tier) and wait for rehydration to complete
You must regenerate the storage account keys to unlock archived data
You must enable the read-access secondary endpoint to read archived blobs

questions.explanation:
**Correct (B):** Archive is an offline tier; its data is not directly readable. To access it you rehydrate the blob — either change its tier to Hot/Cool or copy it to an online tier — and wait for rehydration (standard priority can take hours). Only then can it be read.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **A** Archived blobs cannot be read directly; an attempt to read fails until rehydration completes.
- **C** Key regeneration affects credentials, not the offline state of archived data.
- **D** RA-GRS read endpoints concern regional redundancy, not the Archive tier's offline nature.
references: AZ-104: Implement and manage storage — access tiers and rehydration

questions.stem: Developers on Linux build machines must copy large numbers of files into a Blob container as part of CI, authenticating with Microsoft Entra identities rather than account keys, and they want maximum throughput with built-in retries. Which tool should they use?

options.text: az storage blob upload-batch is impossible on Linux; they must use the Windows-only Storage Explorer
The Azure portal upload blade, scripted with a browser automation tool
AzCopy, signing in with 'azcopy login' to use Microsoft Entra credentials
RoboCopy pointed at the blob endpoint

questions.explanation:
**Correct (C):** AzCopy is the cross-platform, high-throughput command-line tool for bulk data transfer to and from Blob/Files. It supports Microsoft Entra authentication via 'azcopy login' (no account key needed) and provides parallelism and automatic retries, ideal for CI on Linux.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **A** The premise is false; multiple CLI tools work on Linux. Storage Explorer is also cross-platform, but the described high-throughput scripted transfer is AzCopy's purpose.
- **B** The portal upload blade is manual and not built for high-throughput scripted bulk transfer.
- **D** RoboCopy is a Windows file-copy utility for SMB/file systems and does not natively authenticate to Blob with Entra identities for bulk transfer.
references: AZ-104: Implement and manage storage — AzCopy data transfer

questions.stem: On-premises Windows file servers must be replaced by a fully managed SMB file share in Azure that domain-joined users can map with a drive letter and authenticate to using their existing Active Directory credentials. Which solution meets this?

options.text: An Azure Blob container mounted with the blob REST API
An Azure file share with identity-based authentication over SMB (AD DS authentication)
A managed disk attached to a jump box and shared informally
A static website hosted in a storage account

questions.explanation:
**Correct (B):** Azure Files provides a fully managed SMB share that can be mapped with a drive letter. With identity-based authentication using on-premises AD DS, domain-joined users authenticate with their existing AD credentials and NTFS permissions are honored, directly replacing on-prem file servers.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **A** Blob is object storage accessed via REST/SDK, not a drive-letter SMB share with AD authentication.
- **C** A managed disk is block storage attached to a single VM, not a shared, managed multi-user file service.
- **D** A static website serves HTTP content and is unrelated to SMB file shares.
references: AZ-104: Implement and manage storage — Azure Files and identity-based authentication

questions.stem: You must deploy identical VM infrastructure to three environments and want a deployment that is declarative and idempotent: re-running it with the same file should not create duplicate resources but should converge the environment to the described state. Which approach best meets this?

options.text: A shell script that runs a sequence of 'az vm create' commands
A scheduled task that recreates the resource group each run
Manually clicking through the portal and exporting screenshots as documentation
A Bicep file deployed with 'az deployment group create'

questions.explanation:
**Correct (D):** Bicep (and ARM templates) are declarative: you describe the desired end state and the deployment engine makes only the changes needed to reach it. Re-deploying the same file is idempotent — existing matching resources are left in place rather than duplicated.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **A** Imperative 'az vm create' scripts are procedural; re-running them can error or create duplicates and they do not converge to a described state.
- **C** Manual portal clicks are neither repeatable nor declarative.
- **B** Recreating the resource group each run is destructive and not idempotent in the intended sense.
references: AZ-104: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources — ARM templates and Bicep

questions.stem: A running VM has an OS disk and one 256 GiB data disk that must be expanded to 1 TiB while preserving data. Which statements about expanding an Azure managed data disk are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: You increase the disk's provisioned size on the managed disk resource (deallocating the VM if the scenario requires it)
After expanding the disk, you must extend the volume/file system inside the guest OS to use the new space
You must delete the existing data disk and create a new 1 TiB disk, restoring data from backup
Changing the VM to a larger SKU automatically grows the attached data disk to 1 TiB

questions.explanation:
**Correct (A, B):** Azure managed disks support in-place capacity expansion: you raise the provisioned size on the disk resource (deallocating the VM when required by the scenario), then extend the volume inside the guest OS so the added space is usable. Data is preserved.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **C** Deleting and recreating the disk is destructive and unnecessary when in-place expansion preserves data.
- **D** Resizing the VM SKU changes compute size only; it does not resize an attached managed data disk.
references: AZ-104: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources — manage disks (expand)

questions.stem: You need VMs that tolerate the failure of an entire Azure datacenter (a physical building) within a region while still keeping all instances in the same region. Which availability construct provides this protection?

options.text: An availability set with multiple fault domains
A proximity placement group
Spreading the VMs across multiple availability zones in the region
Putting all VMs in a single update domain

questions.explanation:
**Correct (C):** Availability zones are physically separate datacenters within a region, each with independent power, cooling, and networking. Distributing VM instances across zones means the loss of one datacenter does not take down the others, giving datacenter-level fault tolerance while staying in-region.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **A** An availability set protects against rack/hardware and maintenance failures within a single datacenter, not the loss of an entire datacenter building.
- **B** A proximity placement group reduces inter-VM latency by co-locating resources — the opposite of spreading across datacenters.
- **D** A single update domain offers no isolation against a datacenter outage.
references: AZ-104: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources — availability sets and zones

questions.stem: A Virtual Machine Scale Set hosting a stateless web tier must add instances when CPU is high and also guarantee at least 2 instances run at all times and never exceed 10. Which autoscale configuration achieves this?

options.text: A scale-out rule on high CPU, plus minimum=2 and maximum=10 in the autoscale profile
Manual scaling set to 2 instances, increased by an administrator when CPU is high
A single instance with vertical scaling to a larger SKU on high CPU
A scale-out rule only, with no min/max defined

questions.explanation:
**Correct (A):** Autoscale on a scale set uses metric-based rules together with instance-limit bounds. A scale-out rule triggered by high CPU handles load, while setting minimum=2 guarantees a floor and maximum=10 enforces a ceiling, satisfying all three requirements.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **B** Manual scaling requires human intervention and does not automatically respond to CPU.
- **C** Vertical scaling of a single instance does not provide the horizontal redundancy of a minimum of 2 instances and is not how VMSS autoscale works.
- **D** Without min/max bounds you cannot guarantee the floor of 2 or the ceiling of 10.
references: AZ-104: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources — VM Scale Sets autoscale

questions.stem: Your team pushed a new container image to an Azure Container Registry named 'acrteam'. An Azure Container Instances deployment must pull this private image without storing a registry username and password in the deployment. What is the recommended approach?

options.text: Make the ACR repository public so no credentials are needed
Enable a system-assigned managed identity on the container group and grant it AcrPull on the registry
Embed the admin user's password as a plain environment variable in the YAML
Copy the image to Docker Hub and pull it anonymously

questions.explanation:
**Correct (B):** Granting the container group a managed identity and assigning it the AcrPull role lets ACI authenticate to the private registry using Azure AD tokens, with no username/password stored in the deployment definition. This is the recommended, secret-free pattern.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **A** Making the repository public exposes the image and is not a credential solution for a private image requirement.
- **C** The ACR admin account is meant for testing only, and embedding its password as plaintext is exactly the credential-in-deployment practice to avoid.
- **D** Copying to Docker Hub publicly defeats the private-image requirement and adds an unmanaged dependency.
references: AZ-104: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources — ACR and ACI with managed identity

questions.stem: An App Service web app runs on a Standard (S1) plan. You must perform a no-downtime release: deploy a new version, validate it on a separate URL, then make it production with the ability to instantly revert if something is wrong. Which feature should you use?

options.text: Scale up the plan to Premium during each deployment
Delete and recreate the web app for each release
FTP the new files directly into the production wwwroot
Deployment slots, deploying to a staging slot and then swapping with production

questions.explanation:
**Correct (D):** Deployment slots let you deploy to a staging slot with its own URL, validate it, then swap it into production. The swap is near-instant and warmed, and because the previous production content moves into the staging slot you can swap back immediately to revert.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **A** Scaling up changes capacity but provides no staged validation or instant rollback.
- **C** Overwriting production files directly causes downtime and offers no validation or rollback.
- **B** Deleting and recreating the app is disruptive and loses configuration and the rollback path.
references: AZ-104: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources — App Service deployment slots

questions.stem: You are evaluating Azure App Service plans for several web apps. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Multiple web apps can share a single App Service plan and its compute resources
Deployment slots and autoscale require at least the Standard tier or higher
