The Free and Shared tiers do not support custom DNS-based scaling and slots
An App Service plan's pricing tier cannot be changed after creation without redeploying the apps

questions.explanation:
**Correct (A, B, C):** Several apps can run on one plan and share its compute (A). Deployment slots and autoscale are features of Standard and higher tiers (B). Free/Shared tiers lack production features such as slots and scale-out (C).

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **D** You can scale an App Service plan up or down between tiers in place without redeploying the apps, so the claim that the tier cannot be changed without redeployment is false.
references: AZ-104: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources — App Service plans and tiers

questions.stem: A microservice runs in containers, must scale to zero when there is no traffic to minimize cost, and must scale out automatically based on the number of concurrent HTTP requests, without you managing any Kubernetes cluster. Which Azure service best fits?

options.text: Azure Container Apps
A single Azure Container Instance container group
Virtual Machine Scale Sets running Docker
An App Service plan on the Basic tier

questions.explanation:
**Correct (A):** Azure Container Apps is a serverless container platform built on KEDA-based event/HTTP scaling. It can scale to zero when idle and scale out on concurrent HTTP requests, all without you operating a Kubernetes cluster.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **B** A single ACI container group does not provide HTTP-driven autoscaling or scale-to-zero orchestration across replicas.
- **C** VMSS with Docker requires you to manage VM infrastructure and does not natively scale to zero on HTTP concurrency.
- **D** The Basic App Service tier does not support autoscale or scale-to-zero behavior.
references: AZ-104: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources — Azure Container Apps

questions.stem: You will build a custom container image and run it in Azure using only Azure-managed tooling (no local Docker). Arrange the steps in the correct order. (Place the steps in sequence.)

options.text: Create an Azure Container Registry to hold the image
Build and push the image into the registry with 'az acr build'
Grant the runtime (e.g., Container Apps or ACI) AcrPull access to the registry
Deploy the container, referencing the image by its registry path and tag

questions.explanation:
**Correct order (A, B, C, D):** First create the ACR that will store the image (A). Use 'az acr build' to build the image server-side and push it into the registry without local Docker (B). Give the compute runtime AcrPull permission to authenticate to the registry (C). Finally deploy the container referencing the image path and tag (D).

A common error is deploying before the runtime has pull permission, which causes image-pull authorization failures, or trying to build locally when the requirement is Azure-managed tooling via 'az acr build'.
references: AZ-104: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources — ACR build and container deployment

questions.stem: You deployed a VM and chose a Standard HDD managed disk for the OS, but boot times and application responsiveness are poor due to slow disk I/O. The workload needs consistent low-latency performance suitable for a production database. Which managed disk type should you change to?

options.text: An unmanaged disk in a general-purpose v2 storage account
Standard HDD with a larger size
Premium SSD
An additional Standard HDD data disk striped with the OS disk

questions.explanation:
**Correct (C):** Premium SSD managed disks deliver consistent low latency and high IOPS/throughput suitable for production and database workloads, directly addressing the slow-disk symptoms. (Ultra Disk is even higher performance but Premium SSD is the standard production choice here.)

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **B** A larger Standard HDD increases capacity and modest performance but remains HDD-class, not the consistent low latency required.
- **A** Unmanaged disks are legacy and do not solve the performance need; Microsoft recommends managed disks.
- **D** You cannot stripe data disks with the OS disk to fix OS-disk latency; the OS disk itself must be a faster tier.
references: AZ-104: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources — managed disk types

questions.stem: VNet-Hub is peered to VNet-Spoke1 and to VNet-Spoke2. Spoke1 VMs cannot reach Spoke2 VMs even though both are peered to the hub. Routing through a hub firewall is configured with user-defined routes. What is the underlying networking reason the spokes cannot reach each other by default?

options.text: VNet peering is not transitive, so Spoke1 and Spoke2 are not connected just because both peer with the hub
Global VNet peering does not allow any private IP traffic between VNets
Peering automatically blocks all traffic unless an NSG explicitly allows the remote VNet
Spoke-to-spoke traffic requires both spokes to share the same address space

questions.explanation:
**Correct (A):** VNet peering is non-transitive. A peering between hub and each spoke does not create connectivity between the spokes. To enable spoke-to-spoke traffic you route through the hub (for example via an NVA/firewall with UDRs and gateway/route propagation) — which is exactly the hub-and-spoke pattern being built.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **B** Global peering does allow private-IP traffic between VNets; non-transitivity, not a blanket block, is the issue.
- **C** Peering does not implicitly block all traffic; NSGs are separate and not the root cause described.
- **D** Peered VNets must have non-overlapping address spaces; sharing address space would actually break connectivity.
references: AZ-104: Implement and manage virtual networking — VNet peering and transitivity

questions.stem: A subnet's NSG has these inbound rules: priority 100 Allow TCP 3389 from a specific admin IP; priority 200 Deny TCP 3389 from any; plus the default rules. An RDP attempt arrives from an unknown internet IP on TCP 3389. What happens and why?

options.text: Allowed, because the Allow rule at priority 100 is evaluated and permits all 3389 traffic
Allowed, because the default rule AllowVnetInBound overrides custom deny rules
Denied, because rules are processed by priority and the priority 200 Deny matches traffic that did not match the more specific priority 100 Allow
Denied, but only if a CanNotDelete lock is also present on the NSG

questions.explanation:
**Correct (C):** NSG rules are evaluated in priority order (lowest number first), and the first matching rule wins. The priority 100 Allow matches only the specific admin source IP, so traffic from an unknown IP does not match it; evaluation continues to the priority 200 Deny for any source on 3389, which matches and blocks the traffic.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **A** The Allow rule is scoped to a single source IP and does not match the unknown internet IP.
- **B** AllowVnetInBound applies to VirtualNetwork-sourced traffic, not internet sources, and does not override the custom Deny for this flow.
- **D** A resource lock has no bearing on NSG traffic evaluation.
references: AZ-104: Implement and manage virtual networking — NSG rule processing

questions.stem: Storage account 'datalakeprod' must be reachable from resources in subnet 'app-subnet' over the Azure backbone using the storage service's public endpoint, restricted so the storage account only accepts traffic from that subnet. You want a lightweight option without provisioning a private IP/NIC in the VNet. Which feature should you use?

options.text: A private endpoint that injects a private IP for the storage account into app-subnet
Global VNet peering between the subnet and the storage account
A site-to-site VPN from the subnet to the storage account
A service endpoint for Microsoft.Storage on app-subnet, plus a storage firewall rule allowing that subnet

questions.explanation:
**Correct (D):** A service endpoint extends the subnet's identity to the storage service over the Azure backbone and lets you add a network rule on the storage firewall that allows only that subnet. It is lightweight — no private IP or NIC is provisioned in the VNet — matching the requirement to keep using the service's public endpoint securely.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **A** A private endpoint does provision a private IP/NIC in the subnet, which the requirement explicitly wants to avoid.
- **C** A VPN is for connecting networks, not for restricting a PaaS storage account to a subnet.
- **B** You cannot peer a subnet with a storage account; peering connects VNets.
references: AZ-104: Implement and manage virtual networking — service endpoints

questions.stem: You host the public DNS zone 'contoso.com' in Azure DNS. You must point 'www.contoso.com' to a third-party CDN hostname 'contoso.azureedge.net' so that resolving www returns the CDN's current addresses. Which record should you create?

options.text: An A record for www pointing to a fixed IP address
A TXT record for www containing contoso.azureedge.net
An MX record for www pointing to the CDN
A CNAME record for www that aliases to contoso.azureedge.net

questions.explanation:
**Correct (D):** A CNAME maps one hostname to another, so 'www.contoso.com' aliases to 'contoso.azureedge.net' and resolution follows the CDN's own records to its current addresses. This is the standard way to point a subdomain at a provider hostname.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **A** An A record hard-codes an IP, which breaks when the CDN changes addresses and does not follow the provider hostname.
- **C** MX records define mail servers, not web hostname aliases.
- **B** TXT records hold arbitrary text for verification/SPF and do not redirect name resolution.
references: AZ-104: Implement and manage virtual networking — Azure DNS records

questions.stem: An internal three-tier app needs to distribute TCP traffic from the web tier across several backend VMs that have only private IP addresses, entirely within the VNet, at Layer 4 with low latency. Which resource should you deploy?

options.text: An internal (private) Standard Load Balancer with a frontend private IP in the VNet
A public Standard Load Balancer with a public frontend IP
Azure Application Gateway in the public tier
Azure Bastion to reach each backend VM

questions.explanation:
**Correct (A):** An internal Load Balancer uses a private frontend IP and distributes Layer-4 (TCP/UDP) traffic to backend VMs entirely inside the VNet with low latency, exactly matching an internal tier-to-tier balancing requirement.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **B** A public Load Balancer exposes a public IP, which is unnecessary and undesirable for purely internal traffic.
- **C** Application Gateway is a Layer-7 web load balancer; the requirement is Layer-4 internal balancing.
- **D** Azure Bastion provides administrative RDP/SSH access, not traffic distribution across a backend pool.
references: AZ-104: Implement and manage virtual networking — Azure Load Balancer (internal)

questions.stem: You are designing NSG and Application Security Group (ASG) usage for a multi-tier workload. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: An ASG lets you group VM network interfaces and reference that group as the source or destination in NSG rules
NSGs can be associated with a subnet, a network interface, or both
Using ASGs as rule sources/destinations avoids hard-coding individual IP addresses in NSG rules
An ASG itself contains the allow/deny rules and replaces the need for an NSG

questions.explanation:
**Correct (A, B, C):** An ASG is a logical grouping of NICs that you reference in NSG rules as source/destination (A). NSGs can attach to a subnet, a NIC, or both, and both apply (B). Referencing ASGs lets rules target roles instead of brittle IP lists (C).

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **D** ASGs hold no rules; they are only groupings. The allow/deny rules still live in an NSG, which references the ASGs. An ASG does not replace an NSG.
references: AZ-104: Implement and manage virtual networking — NSGs and application security groups

questions.stem: A subnet contains VMs that must send all outbound internet traffic through a network virtual appliance (NVA) at 10.0.100.4 for inspection. You create a route table with a route 0.0.0.0/0 -> Virtual appliance (next hop 10.0.100.4) and associate it with the subnet, but traffic still goes directly to the internet. Besides associating the route table, what is most likely required?

options.text: Move the NVA into the same subnet as the VMs
Delete the default system route, because user-defined routes cannot coexist with system routes
Add a public IP to every VM so the route can take effect
Enable IP forwarding on the NVA's network interface so it can route traffic that is not addressed to itself

questions.explanation:
**Correct (D):** For an NVA to forward packets whose destination is not its own IP, IP forwarding must be enabled on the NVA's NIC (and the guest OS must be configured to forward). Without it, the appliance drops the redirected traffic, so even a correct UDR appears not to work.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **B** UDRs coexist with and override system routes by longest-prefix/precedence; you do not (and cannot) delete the system default route this way.
- **C** Public IPs on the VMs are not required for the UDR to redirect egress through the NVA.
- **A** The NVA does not need to be in the same subnet; it just needs reachability and IP forwarding enabled.
references: AZ-104: Implement and manage virtual networking — user-defined routes and NVAs

questions.stem: Administrators must open RDP/SSH sessions to VMs that have no public IP addresses, directly from the Azure portal over TLS, without deploying or managing a jump-box VM. Which service provides this?

options.text: Azure Bastion deployed into the VNet
A public IP and an NSG rule allowing 3389/22 from the internet
A site-to-site VPN for each administrator
Azure Load Balancer inbound NAT rules to the VMs

questions.explanation:
**Correct (A):** Azure Bastion is a managed PaaS service deployed into the VNet that brokers RDP/SSH from the Azure portal over TLS to VMs using their private IPs, with no public IP on the VMs and no jump box to manage.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **B** Assigning public IPs and opening 3389/22 to the internet is the insecure pattern Bastion is designed to eliminate.
- **C** A per-admin VPN is heavier to manage and not the portal-based brokered access described.
- **D** Inbound NAT rules still require exposing endpoints and do not provide the managed, portal-integrated secure access Bastion does.
references: AZ-104: Implement and manage virtual networking — Azure Bastion

questions.stem: You configured a metric alert on a VM for high CPU and want it to email the on-call team and also trigger an Azure Function for automated remediation. You do not want to duplicate notification settings across multiple alerts. What should you configure as the alert's response target?

options.text: An action group containing an email action and an Azure Function action, referenced by the alert rule
A separate alert rule for the email and another for the function
A diagnostic setting that forwards the metric to Log Analytics
A budget alert in Cost Management

questions.explanation:
**Correct (A):** An action group bundles one or more actions (email, SMS, webhook, Azure Function, Logic App, etc.) and is referenced by alert rules. Multiple alerts can reuse the same action group, so notification and remediation settings are defined once and not duplicated.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **B** Creating separate alert rules duplicates configuration and is the opposite of reuse.
- **C** A diagnostic setting routes telemetry to a destination; it does not send notifications or run remediation in response to an alert.
- **D** A Cost Management budget alert concerns spend thresholds, not VM CPU metric responses.
references: AZ-104: Monitor and maintain Azure resources — alerts and action groups

questions.stem: A VM cannot reach an external endpoint, and you must determine the next hop Azure applies for a given destination IP from that VM's NIC — distinguishing whether traffic goes to the internet, a virtual appliance, or is dropped. Which Network Watcher capability should you use?

options.text: IP flow verify
Next hop
Connection troubleshoot only
Packet capture

questions.explanation:
**Correct (B):** The Network Watcher Next hop tool takes a source VM/NIC and a destination IP and returns the next hop type Azure's routing applies (Internet, Virtual appliance, VnetLocal, None/dropped, etc.), which is exactly how you diagnose where routing sends or drops the traffic.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **A** IP flow verify checks whether NSG rules allow or deny a specific flow; it reports the rule decision, not the routing next hop.
- **C** Connection troubleshoot tests end-to-end connectivity but does not specifically return the routing next-hop type for an arbitrary destination the way Next hop does.
- **D** Packet capture records packets for deep analysis; it is heavier and not the direct way to read the computed next hop.
references: AZ-104: Monitor and maintain Azure resources — Network Watcher next hop

questions.stem: You protect Azure VMs with Azure Backup using a Recovery Services vault. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: A backup policy defines the backup schedule and how long recovery points are retained
You can restore an entire VM or restore individual files from a recovery point
The Recovery Services vault can store backups with locally redundant or geo-redundant storage
Azure Backup requires you to stop (deallocate) the VM during every scheduled backup

questions.explanation:
**Correct (A, B, C):** A backup policy sets schedule and retention (A). From a recovery point you can restore the whole VM or use file-level recovery to retrieve individual files (B). The vault's backup storage redundancy can be LRS or GRS (C).

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **D** Azure Backup performs application-consistent backups of running VMs using snapshots and the VM agent; it does not require deallocating the VM for each backup.
references: AZ-104: Monitor and maintain Azure resources — Azure Backup and Recovery Services vault

questions.stem: You enable Azure Site Recovery to replicate production VMs from East US to West US. Before declaring real DR readiness, you must validate that VMs come up correctly in West US without affecting the ongoing replication or the production workload. Which action should you perform?

options.text: Run a test failover into an isolated network in the secondary region
Run a planned failover to West US and run production there for a day
Disable replication, boot the VMs in West US, then re-enable replication
Delete the source VMs to force the recovery VMs to start

questions.explanation:
**Correct (A):** A test failover (DR drill) spins up the replicated VMs in an isolated network in the secondary region so you can validate boot and application health. It does not impact ongoing replication or the running production VMs, making it the correct non-disruptive validation.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **B** A planned failover actually moves the workload to the secondary region, which is disruptive and not a non-impacting validation.
- **C** Disabling replication breaks protection and loses the recovery position; it is not how you test.
- **D** Deleting source VMs is destructive and defeats the purpose of validating DR readiness.
references: AZ-104: Monitor and maintain Azure resources — Azure Site Recovery test failover

questions.stem: A help-desk team must be able to reset passwords and manage multi-factor authentication settings for standard users in Microsoft Entra ID, but they must NOT be able to modify administrator accounts or change group memberships. Which built-in Entra role follows least privilege?

options.text: User Administrator
Helpdesk Administrator (Password Administrator role family)
Authentication Administrator
Global Administrator

questions.explanation:
**Correct (C):** The Authentication Administrator role can reset passwords and manage authentication methods (including MFA) for non-admin users, but cannot manage members in administrator roles or alter group memberships. That precisely fits the requirement.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **A** User Administrator can create and manage users and groups (including memberships), which exceeds the requirement of not changing group membership.
- **B** The Helpdesk/Password Administrator can reset passwords for limited roles but does not own the broader MFA authentication-method management scope the way Authentication Administrator does, and the requirement explicitly includes managing MFA settings.
- **D** Global Administrator grants full tenant control, the opposite of least privilege.
references: AZ-104: Manage Azure identities and governance — Entra built-in roles

questions.stem: You need to allow users from a partner organization to access a SharePoint site and a couple of internal apps in your tenant. The partners should sign in with their own existing work credentials, and you must not create or manage passwords for them. What should you implement?

options.text: Invite the partners as Microsoft Entra B2B guest users
Create cloud-only member accounts for each partner in your tenant
Configure Microsoft Entra Domain Services and join the partners' devices
Add the partners' domain as a custom domain in your tenant

questions.explanation:
**Correct (A):** Microsoft Entra B2B collaboration invites external users as guests. They authenticate against their home tenant/identity provider, so you never manage their credentials, and you grant them access to specific apps and resources in your tenant.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **B** Creating member accounts means you own and manage those identities and passwords, which the requirement forbids.
- **C** Entra Domain Services provides managed domain (LDAP/Kerberos) services for legacy workloads; it does not federate external partner identities for app access.
- **D** Adding a custom domain proves you own a DNS domain for your own tenant; it does not let external partners sign in with their own credentials.
references: AZ-104: Manage Azure identities and governance — external identities (B2B)

questions.stem: A custom RBAC role contains the action 'Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/*' under Actions and 'Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/listKeys/action' under NotActions. A user assigned this role at a storage account tries to list the account keys. What is the result, and why?

options.text: Allowed, because the wildcard in Actions grants every storage operation
Denied, because NotActions always overrides any Owner assignment at a higher scope
Allowed, because NotActions only applies to DataActions, not Actions
Denied, because an action listed in NotActions is subtracted from the granted Actions

questions.explanation:
**Correct (D):** Effective permissions for an Azure role are Actions minus NotActions. The wildcard grants all storage account control-plane actions, but listKeys is explicitly removed by NotActions, so that specific operation is not permitted by this role.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **A** The wildcard would grant listKeys, but NotActions subtracts it; you must evaluate both.
- **B** NotActions reduces only the permissions of the role that contains it; it does not override a separate Owner assignment granted elsewhere. The user here is only assigned this custom role.
- **C** NotActions applies to the management (control-plane) Actions set; DataActions has its own NotDataActions. listKeys is a control-plane action and is correctly excluded.
references: AZ-104: Manage Azure identities and governance — custom roles, Actions/NotActions

questions.stem: Company policy requires that every resource group created in the Production subscription must carry a 'Department' tag, and resource group creation should be blocked outright if the tag is missing. Which Azure Policy effect should the assignment use?

options.text: Append
Modify
Deny
Audit

questions.explanation:
**Correct (C):** Deny evaluates the request and rejects the create/update operation when the condition (tag absent) is met, so a resource group without the Department tag cannot be created. That satisfies 'blocked outright'.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **A** Append adds a field/value to the request but does not block; if no default value is supplied it does not enforce that the user provides one.
- **B** Modify adds, updates, or removes tags (often used with remediation) rather than blocking creation.
- **D** Audit only flags non-compliance in reports; it never prevents the operation.
references: AZ-104: Manage Azure identities and governance — Azure Policy effects

questions.stem: You are designing a Microsoft Entra Conditional Access strategy for AZ-104 administrative tasks. Which statements about Conditional Access are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Conditional Access policies are evaluated after first-factor authentication succeeds and can require MFA based on signals such as user, location, and device state
You can require that access to the Azure management endpoints (the 'Microsoft Azure Management' app) be granted only from compliant or hybrid-joined devices
Report-only mode lets you evaluate the impact of a policy on sign-ins without enforcing the controls
Conditional Access requires Azure Policy to be assigned at the subscription scope before it can take effect
Conditional Access can replace Azure RBAC for authorizing which actions a user can perform on a resource

questions.explanation:
**Correct (A, B, C):** Conditional Access runs after the first factor and uses signals (user, group, location, device, risk) to grant, block, or require additional controls such as MFA (A). A common admin-protection pattern targets the Microsoft Azure Management cloud app and requires a compliant/hybrid-joined device (B). Report-only mode evaluates and logs what a policy would do without enforcing it, ideal for safe rollout (C).

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **D** Conditional Access is an Entra ID feature and does not depend on an Azure Policy assignment to function.
- **E** Conditional Access governs access conditions at sign-in; it does not authorize per-resource actions. Azure RBAC determines what actions an identity may perform.
references: AZ-104: Manage Azure identities and governance — Conditional Access

questions.stem: Several teams keep deleting each other's resources by accident. You want one mechanism that, applied at a resource group, allows people to read and use the resources but blocks modification and deletion of everything in that group, regardless of their RBAC role. What should you apply?

options.text: A CanNotDelete lock on the resource group
A ReadOnly lock on the resource group
An Azure Policy with the Deny effect on writes
Remove Contributor and assign Reader to every user

questions.explanation:
**Correct (B):** A ReadOnly lock prevents all create, update, and delete operations on resources in its scope (and child resources), while still allowing read. It overrides RBAC for those operations, so even Owners cannot modify or delete.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **A** A CanNotDelete lock blocks deletion but still allows modification (writes), so it does not stop accidental changes.
- **C** A Deny policy can block writes, but a ReadOnly lock is the single, simpler mechanism that blocks both modify and delete and is the intended governance tool here; crafting policy rules for every resource type is far more error-prone.
- **D** RBAC changes do not stop an Owner, and the requirement is a single mechanism that overrides role membership.
references: AZ-104: Manage Azure identities and governance — resource locks

questions.stem: Your finance team wants a consolidated view of month-to-date cost broken down by resource group and by tag, with the ability to filter by service and export the results. Which Azure tool should they use?

options.text: Microsoft Cost Management — Cost analysis
Azure Advisor
Azure Monitor Metrics
Azure Policy compliance

questions.explanation:
**Correct (A):** Cost analysis in Microsoft Cost Management provides interactive month-to-date and historical cost views, with grouping and filtering by resource group, tag, service, and more, plus export.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **B** Azure Advisor gives recommendations (including cost-saving tips) but is not the detailed cost-breakdown explorer.
- **C** Azure Monitor Metrics tracks performance/health telemetry, not billing cost.
- **D** Azure Policy compliance reports on policy adherence, unrelated to spend reporting.
references: AZ-104: Manage Azure identities and governance — Cost Management

questions.stem: A management group hierarchy has Tenant Root > MG-Corp > MG-Prod. An Azure Policy assigned at MG-Corp denies creation of public IP addresses. A subscription under MG-Prod needs a temporary exception for one resource group to deploy a public IP for a migration, while keeping the deny everywhere else. What is the cleanest supported approach?

options.text: Delete the policy assignment at MG-Corp for the duration of the migration
Override the assignment with a second Allow policy at the resource group
Move the subscription out of the management group hierarchy temporarily
Create a policy exemption scoped to that specific resource group for the assignment

questions.explanation:
**Correct (D):** A policy exemption is the supported way to exclude a specific scope (here, the resource group) from a particular assignment for a period of time, without affecting the deny everywhere else. Exemptions can carry an expiration and a justification.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **A** Deleting the assignment removes the deny for the entire MG-Corp subtree, exposing everything, not just the one resource group.
- **B** Azure Policy has no 'Allow' effect that overrides a Deny; Deny cannot be cancelled by a competing assignment.
- **C** Moving the subscription disrupts all inherited governance and other policies, and is far more invasive than an exemption.
references: AZ-104: Manage Azure identities and governance — policy exemptions, management groups

questions.stem: You manage role assignments with Azure RBAC across subscriptions. Which statements about Azure RBAC scope and inheritance are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: A role assigned at a subscription is inherited by all resource groups and resources within that subscription
Azure RBAC permissions are additive across assignments, except where a deny assignment explicitly removes an action
Assigning a role at a resource group does not grant any permissions to resources in a sibling resource group
An assignment made at a child resource group can be inherited upward to its parent subscription
Only the Owner role can be assigned at the management group scope

questions.explanation:
**Correct (A, B, C):** RBAC inheritance flows downward from management group to subscription to resource group to resource, so a subscription-level assignment applies to everything beneath it (A). Effective access is the union of all assignments, minus any deny assignments (B). Scope is hierarchical and lateral isolation holds: a resource-group assignment does not reach a sibling resource group (C).

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **D** Inheritance is downward only; a child assignment never propagates up to the parent.
- **E** Most built-in roles (Reader, Contributor, Owner, and many resource-specific ones) can be assigned at the management group scope, not just Owner.
references: AZ-104: Manage Azure identities and governance — RBAC scope and inheritance

questions.stem: You need a Microsoft Entra group whose membership is updated automatically based on each user's 'accountEnabled' and 'department' attributes, and the membership must include nested device objects as well. Which statement correctly describes the limitation you must account for?

options.text: Dynamic membership rules cannot reference the department attribute
Dynamic groups can contain users OR devices, but a single dynamic group cannot mix both object types
Dynamic groups support nested group membership for assigned members
Dynamic membership only works for security groups created in on-premises Active Directory

questions.explanation:
**Correct (B):** A dynamic membership group targets a single object type — either users or devices — chosen when the rule is created. You cannot have one dynamic group whose rule populates both users and devices, so you would create two groups.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **A** Department is a standard user attribute fully usable in membership rules.
- **C** Dynamic groups are populated by a rule, not by manually nested members; and dynamic group rules do not evaluate nested group membership.
- **D** Dynamic membership is a cloud Entra ID feature and does not require groups originate in on-premises AD; it commonly requires appropriate Entra ID licensing.
references: AZ-104: Manage Azure identities and governance — dynamic groups

questions.stem: You must create a custom Azure RBAC role from scratch using the Azure CLI and assign it to a user at a resource group. Arrange the high-level steps in the correct order. (Place the steps in sequence.)

options.text: Author a role definition JSON file listing Actions, NotActions, and AssignableScopes
Run 'az role definition create' with that JSON file to register the custom role
Using the registered role's name, gather the user's object ID and the target resource-group scope
Run 'az role assignment create' with the role name, object ID, and scope to assign it

questions.explanation:
**Correct order (A, B, C, D):** First write the role definition JSON, declaring the permitted Actions/NotActions and the AssignableScopes where the role may be used (A). Register it with 'az role definition create' so the custom role exists in the directory (B). Gather the assignee's object ID and the resource group scope you will target (C). Finally bind the role to the user at that scope with 'az role assignment create' (D).

A frequent mistake is attempting the assignment before the role definition is created, or omitting the resource group from AssignableScopes, which then blocks assigning the role there.
references: AZ-104: Manage Azure identities and governance — custom RBAC roles via CLI

questions.stem: An Azure Storage account is configured as Zone-redundant storage (ZRS) in a single region. A whole Azure region suffers a prolonged outage. What is the data-availability outcome you should expect?

options.text: Data remains available because ZRS keeps an asynchronous copy in a paired region
Data automatically fails over to a secondary region after one hour
Data may be unavailable, because ZRS replicates only across availability zones within the same region
Data remains available because ZRS keeps three copies in a single datacenter

questions.explanation:
**Correct (C):** ZRS synchronously replicates across three availability zones within one region. It protects against a datacenter/zone failure, but if the entire region is down there is no copy elsewhere, so data can be unavailable. Cross-region protection requires GRS/GZRS.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **A** ZRS has no secondary-region copy; that is the geo-redundant family (GRS/GZRS).
- **B** ZRS does not perform cross-region failover; only geo-redundant accounts support failover to a secondary region.
- **D** LRS keeps three copies in one datacenter; ZRS specifically spreads copies across zones, which is what gives it zone resilience.
references: AZ-104: Implement and manage storage — redundancy (ZRS)

questions.stem: You must give a mobile app limited, expiring access to upload blobs to several different storage accounts, and you want to centrally revoke that access at any time without regenerating account keys. Which approach best meets these requirements?

options.text: Use a user delegation SAS signed with Microsoft Entra credentials
Distribute account key 2 to the app and rotate it when revocation is needed
Use a service SAS tied to a stored access policy on each container
Make the containers public with anonymous write access

questions.explanation:
**Correct (A):** A user delegation SAS is signed using an Entra ID credential (a user delegation key) rather than the account key. It is the recommended, more secure SAS form, has an enforced maximum lifetime, and you can revoke it centrally by revoking the user delegation keys — without touching account keys.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **B** Sharing an account key gives full access and the only revocation is key rotation, which disrupts every other consumer.
- **C** A service SAS with stored access policies allows revocation, but it is signed by the account key (not Entra), so it is less secure and revocation is per-container policy, not centralized via identity.
- **D** Anonymous write is a serious security risk and provides no expiry or per-app control.
references: AZ-104: Implement and manage storage — shared access signatures

questions.stem: A Linux web server farm needs a shared POSIX-compliant file system that multiple VMs can mount concurrently using the NFS protocol. Which Azure Files configuration should you choose?

options.text: An Azure NetApp Files volume is the only option that supports any file sharing
A standard general-purpose v2 file share using SMB 3.0
A blob container mounted with BlobFuse
A premium file share (FileStorage account) using the NFS 4.1 protocol

questions.explanation:
**Correct (D):** Azure Files supports NFS 4.1 on premium file shares, which are hosted in a FileStorage (premium) account. That delivers the concurrent, POSIX-style shared file system Linux hosts need over NFS.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **A** Azure NetApp Files is a separate high-performance option, but it is not the 'only' way to get NFS file sharing — Azure Files premium provides NFS 4.1 too.
- **B** Standard general-purpose v2 file shares use SMB; the NFS protocol on Azure Files requires the premium tier.
- **C** BlobFuse mounts blob storage as a filesystem but is object storage underneath, not a true NFS file share with full file semantics.
references: AZ-104: Implement and manage storage — Azure Files NFS

questions.stem: You are reviewing data-protection features on a general-purpose v2 storage account. Which statements about blob versioning, snapshots, and soft delete are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Enabling blob versioning is mutually exclusive with enabling blob soft delete on the same account
Blob versioning automatically creates a new version when a blob is modified or deleted, preserving prior content
Container soft delete lets you restore a deleted container within the configured retention period
A blob snapshot is a read-only point-in-time copy of a blob that you create explicitly
Point-in-time restore for block blobs requires that versioning, change feed, and blob soft delete all be disabled

questions.explanation:
**Correct (B, C, D):** Versioning captures a prior version automatically on each write/delete so earlier content is retained (B). Container soft delete allows restoring an accidentally deleted container during its retention window (C). A snapshot is an explicit, read-only point-in-time copy of a single blob (D).

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **A** Versioning and blob soft delete are complementary and can both be enabled on the same account; they protect against different mistakes.
- **E** Point-in-time restore actually requires versioning, change feed, and blob soft delete to be ENABLED, not disabled.
references: AZ-104: Implement and manage storage — versioning, snapshots, soft delete

questions.stem: A blob lifecycle management rule moves blobs to Cool after 30 days and to Archive after 90 days based on last modification. A team complains that some recently re-read blobs were still archived. What correctly explains the behavior?

options.text: Lifecycle rules use last-access time only, so reads should have reset the timer
The rule's condition is daysAfterModificationGreaterThan, so reading a blob does not reset the move timer
Archive tiering cannot be driven by lifecycle policy and must be manual
Lifecycle policies evaluate continuously in real time, so the delay indicates a misconfiguration

questions.explanation:
**Correct (B):** The rule uses daysAfterModificationGreaterThan, which is based on the last-modified timestamp. Merely reading a blob does not change last-modified, so reads do not reset the clock and the blobs still age into Archive. To react to reads you must enable last-access tracking and use daysAfterLastAccessTimeGreaterThan.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **A** This rule is not configured on last-access time; that is a different, opt-in condition requiring access-time tracking.
- **C** Lifecycle policies can tier blobs to Archive automatically; that is a core use case.
- **D** Lifecycle policy runs on a periodic schedule (it can take up to about a day to take effect), so a delay is expected, not a misconfiguration.
references: AZ-104: Implement and manage storage — lifecycle management

questions.stem: You must mount an Azure Files SMB share on an on-premises Windows server, but corporate firewalls block outbound TCP 445. You cannot open 445 to the internet. Which solution lets the server reach the file share?

options.text: Switch the share to the NFS protocol, which uses port 2049
Enable the storage account's public endpoint and use TCP 443 for SMB
Establish a Site-to-Site VPN or ExpressRoute and access the share over a private endpoint / private IP
Use AzCopy, which tunnels SMB over HTTPS automatically

questions.explanation:
**Correct (C):** SMB requires TCP 445. When the internet path on 445 is blocked, you keep the traffic off the public internet by connecting over a Site-to-Site VPN or ExpressRoute and reaching the share through a private endpoint (private IP) inside your network, where 445 is permitted internally.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **A** NFS shares on Azure Files are not supported for Windows SMB clients in this scenario and have their own networking requirements; the requirement is the existing SMB share.
- **B** SMB does not run over 443; the storage HTTPS endpoint (443) is for REST/blob, not SMB file mounting.
- **D** AzCopy is a data-copy tool over HTTPS, not a way to mount and use an SMB share with a drive letter.
references: AZ-104: Implement and manage storage — Azure Files networking

questions.stem: An archived block blob must be made readable as quickly as possible for an urgent audit, and cost is a secondary concern. You initiate rehydration. Which choice gives the fastest path to read the data?

options.text: Set rehydrate priority to High when changing the blob's tier to Hot/Cool
Set rehydrate priority to Standard when changing the blob's tier to Hot/Cool
Read the blob directly from the Archive tier without rehydration
Enable the storage account's geo-redundancy to accelerate retrieval

questions.explanation:
**Correct (A):** Rehydrating from Archive to an online tier (Hot/Cool) is required before the data is readable, and you can set rehydrate priority to High to prioritize the operation for faster completion when time matters more than cost.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **B** Standard priority is slower (can take many hours); High priority is the faster option.
- **C** Archive is offline; you cannot read the blob until it is rehydrated to an online tier.
- **D** Geo-redundancy affects durability/availability across regions, not Archive rehydration speed.
references: AZ-104: Implement and manage storage — archive rehydration

questions.stem: Developers need to browse, upload, and download blobs and manage file shares on several storage accounts from their Windows and macOS laptops using a graphical tool, authenticating with their Entra ID accounts. Which tool should you recommend?

options.text: Azure Data Box
Azure Cloud Shell
AzCopy
Azure Storage Explorer

questions.explanation:
**Correct (D):** Azure Storage Explorer is the cross-platform GUI for managing blobs, files, queues, and tables across multiple accounts, and it supports signing in with Microsoft Entra accounts as well as keys/SAS.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **A** Azure Data Box is a physical appliance for bulk offline data transfer, not a laptop management tool.
- **B** Cloud Shell is a browser-based command-line environment, not a graphical storage browser.
- **C** AzCopy is a powerful command-line copy utility, not a GUI for browsing and managing shares.
references: AZ-104: Implement and manage storage — management tools

questions.stem: You are configuring network security for a storage account using its firewall and the 'Public network access' settings. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: When the firewall is set to deny by default, you can still allow access from selected virtual network subnets via service endpoints
Configuring the storage firewall automatically deletes all existing access keys
Adding a private endpoint assigns the storage account a private IP inside your VNet, and traffic to it stays on the Microsoft backbone
The 'Allow Azure services on the trusted services list to access this storage account' exception can grant trusted Microsoft services access even when public access is restricted
IP network rules on the storage firewall accept private RFC 1918 source addresses from the internet

questions.explanation:
**Correct (A, C, D):** With a default-deny firewall you can permit specific VNet subnets using service endpoints (A). A private endpoint projects the account into your VNet with a private IP and keeps traffic on the Azure backbone (C). The trusted-services exception lets allowlisted Microsoft services reach the account even when public access is otherwise locked down (D).

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **B** Configuring the firewall does not touch or delete access keys; key management is separate.
- **E** Storage firewall IP rules are for public IP addresses; you cannot use them to allow private RFC 1918 addresses, which are not routable on the public internet.
references: AZ-104: Implement and manage storage — storage firewall and endpoints

questions.stem: You deploy two VMs into the same availability set with two fault domains and five update domains. What guarantee does the availability set provide?

options.text: The VMs are spread across separate Azure regions for geographic redundancy
The VMs are placed in different fault and update domains so a single rack failure or planned host update does not take both down
The VMs are guaranteed to survive an entire region outage
The VMs receive a 99.999% connectivity SLA for a single instance

questions.explanation:
**Correct (B):** An availability set distributes VMs across fault domains (separate power/network/racks) and update domains (separate maintenance groups). With two VMs in two fault domains, a single rack/power failure or a host update cycle will not affect both at once.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **A** Availability sets are within a single datacenter/region; they do not span regions.
- **C** Surviving a full region outage requires cross-region designs (paired regions, ASR); an availability set does not.
- **D** The higher SLA applies to multi-VM configurations; a single VM has its own (lower) SLA, and the five-nines figure is not what an availability set provides.
references: AZ-104: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources — availability sets

questions.stem: You must deploy VMs that tolerate a full datacenter (zone) failure within a region. The deployment should automatically distribute instances across zones and let you add or remove instances based on load. Which compute option best fits?

options.text: An availability set in a single zone
A single large VM with Premium SSD disks
A Virtual Machine Scale Set configured to spread across availability zones
A proximity placement group

questions.explanation:
**Correct (C):** A Virtual Machine Scale Set can be configured to spread instances across availability zones, giving zone resilience, and it natively supports scaling instances in and out based on metrics or schedules.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **A** An availability set protects against rack-level failures within one datacenter but is not zone-redundant and does not auto-scale.
- **B** A single VM has no redundancy and cannot scale out across instances.
- **D** A proximity placement group co-locates resources for low latency — the opposite of spreading across zones — and does not provide scaling.
references: AZ-104: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources — VMSS and zones

questions.stem: An Azure App Service web app on a Standard plan must run a nightly maintenance script and a scheduled cleanup job, hosted within the same app without provisioning separate compute. Which App Service feature should you use?

options.text: WebJobs
Deployment slots
Scale-out (autoscale) rules
Hybrid Connections

questions.explanation:
**Correct (A):** WebJobs let you run background scripts and scheduled (cron-style) jobs inside an existing App Service app, with no separate compute, which matches running nightly maintenance and cleanup tasks.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **B** Deployment slots provide staging/swap for releases, not scheduled background processing.
- **C** Autoscale changes instance count based on load; it does not run scheduled jobs.
- **D** Hybrid Connections give secure access from the app to on-premises resources; they do not schedule jobs.
references: AZ-104: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources — App Service WebJobs

questions.stem: You want to deploy a single container quickly for a short-lived test, billed per second, without managing any VMs or orchestrators, and you do not need scaling or load balancing. Which service is the best fit?

options.text: Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS)
Azure App Service
Azure Virtual Machine Scale Sets
Azure Container Instances (ACI)

questions.explanation:
**Correct (D):** Azure Container Instances runs a single container (or container group) on demand with per-second billing and no infrastructure or orchestrator to manage — ideal for short-lived, simple workloads.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **A** AKS is a managed Kubernetes orchestrator; it is heavyweight for a single throwaway container.
- **B** App Service is for web apps/APIs; while it can host containers, ACI is the simpler per-second, run-and-forget choice described here.
- **C** VMSS manages fleets of VMs, not individual containers, and requires VM management.
references: AZ-104: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources — ACI

questions.stem: You are authoring Bicep and ARM template deployments for repeatable infrastructure. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Bicep requires you to manually manage resource creation order by writing explicit sequence numbers
Bicep is transpiled into ARM JSON before being submitted to Azure Resource Manager
ARM template and Bicep deployments are idempotent: deploying the same template again converges resources to the declared state rather than duplicating them
Parameters cannot be supplied at deployment time and must be hard-coded in the template
Deployment scope can be set to resource group, subscription, management group, or tenant

questions.explanation:
**Correct (B, C, E):** Bicep compiles down to ARM JSON, which Resource Manager actually processes (B). Both are declarative and idempotent, so re-deploying converges to the desired state without creating duplicates (C). Deployments can target resource group, subscription, management group, or tenant scope (E).

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **A** Bicep infers most dependencies automatically from references and supports dependsOn when needed; you do not assign manual sequence numbers.
- **D** Parameters are designed to be supplied at deployment time (CLI, portal, parameter files), enabling reuse across environments.
references: AZ-104: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources — ARM/Bicep

questions.stem: A running Azure VM must be resized to a larger SKU. The target SKU is supported on the VM's current host hardware cluster. What is the expected behavior when you change the size in the portal?

options.text: The resize is blocked because resizing always requires deleting and recreating the VM
The VM is restarted (stopped and started) to apply the new size, causing a brief outage
The size changes live with zero restart because the SKU is available on the host
You must first move the VM to a different region before resizing

questions.explanation:
**Correct (B):** Changing a VM size requires a restart — Azure stops the VM, applies the new size, and starts it again, producing a brief outage. When the target SKU is available on the current host cluster, this is straightforward and does not force a deallocate-to-new-host scenario.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **A** Resizing does not require deleting/recreating the VM; the size property is updated in place.
- **C** Resizing is not zero-restart; a reboot occurs even when the SKU is on the same cluster.
- **D** Moving regions is unnecessary; if the SKU were unavailable on the cluster you would deallocate and resize, but not change region.
references: AZ-104: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources — VM resize

questions.stem: An Azure Container Apps environment hosts an HTTP microservice. Traffic is highly variable, often zero overnight, and you want to minimize cost while still handling bursts, without managing Kubernetes. Which scaling configuration meets this?

options.text: Set a fixed minimum of three replicas at all times
Migrate the workload to a single VM with a startup script
Enable scale-to-zero by setting minimum replicas to 0 and configure an HTTP-based scale rule
Use a CPU metric on a VM Scale Set with a minimum of two instances

questions.explanation:
**Correct (C):** Azure Container Apps supports scale-to-zero. Setting minimum replicas to 0 means no replicas (and minimal cost) when idle, and an HTTP scale rule adds replicas to handle incoming requests during bursts — all without managing Kubernetes.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **A** A fixed minimum of three replicas runs continuously and wastes cost during idle periods.
- **B** A single VM cannot scale out for bursts and keeps running (and billing) overnight.
- **D** A VMSS with a two-instance minimum still runs at least two VMs continuously and requires VM management; it does not scale to zero.
references: AZ-104: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources — Container Apps scaling

questions.stem: You manage an Azure Container Registry. A new requirement says only images that have passed scanning may be deployed, and you want to prevent images from being overwritten once pushed with a given tag, while keeping a record of changes. Which ACR capability addresses tag overwrite protection?

options.text: Enable image (tag) locking / repository immutability so a pushed tag cannot be overwritten or deleted
Enable the Premium SKU's geo-replication
Switch the registry to anonymous pull access
Reduce the registry to the Basic SKU to disable overwrites

questions.explanation:
**Correct (A):** ACR lets you lock individual images/tags (set them to read-only / disable delete and write) so a pushed tag cannot be overwritten or removed, preserving the exact artifact that was scanned.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **B** Geo-replication copies the registry across regions for locality/resilience; it does not prevent tag overwrites.
- **C** Anonymous pull weakens security and is unrelated to immutability.
- **D** The Basic SKU does not provide immutability and reducing SKU does not disable overwrites; locking is the correct control.
references: AZ-104: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources — ACR image locking

questions.stem: You are evaluating Azure App Service deployment slots for a production web app. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Swapping slots exchanges the running content and warms up the target slot to reduce downtime during release
Slot-specific (sticky) settings can be marked so they stay with a slot and do not swap
Each deployment slot must run on its own separate App Service plan and is billed separately
After a swap you cannot revert, so a bad release requires redeploying from source
Deployment slots are available on Standard, Premium, and Isolated App Service plans

questions.explanation:
**Correct (A, B, E):** A swap exchanges the contents of two slots and pre-warms the target to minimize downtime (A). You can mark settings as slot-sticky so they remain with the slot instead of moving during a swap (B). Slots are a feature of Standard and higher plans (Standard, Premium, Isolated) (E).

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **C** Slots run on the same App Service plan as the app, sharing its compute; they are not separate plans billed individually.
- **D** A swap is reversible — you can simply swap back to restore the previous production content quickly.
references: AZ-104: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources — App Service slots

questions.stem: A VM uses a Standard HDD OS disk and suffers slow, inconsistent I/O. The workload needs predictable, single-digit-millisecond latency and high IOPS for a production database. Which managed disk type should you move to?

options.text: Standard SSD
An unmanaged page blob disk
Standard HDD with host caching enabled
Premium SSD

questions.explanation:
**Correct (D):** Premium SSD delivers consistent low-latency, high-IOPS performance suited to production databases and I/O-intensive workloads (Ultra Disk is the even higher tier when extreme performance is required).

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **A** Standard SSD improves consistency over HDD but does not match Premium SSD's low latency and IOPS for demanding production databases.
- **B** Unmanaged disks are legacy and add management burden; managed Premium SSD is the recommended, supported choice.
- **C** Host caching helps, but the underlying Standard HDD still cannot guarantee the latency/IOPS a production database needs.
references: AZ-104: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources — managed disk types

questions.stem: You will deploy a Linux web VM behind a public Standard Load Balancer using the Azure portal. Arrange the high-level steps in the correct order. (Place the steps in sequence.)

options.text: Create the virtual network and subnet
Create the Standard Load Balancer with a public frontend IP and an empty backend pool
Create the VM, attach its NIC to the subnet, and add that NIC to the load balancer's backend pool
Configure the health probe and load-balancing rule, then verify traffic reaches the VM

questions.explanation:
**Correct order (A, B, C, D):** First provide the network foundation by creating the VNet and subnet (A). Create the Standard Load Balancer with a public frontend IP and an empty backend pool (B). Deploy the VM, connect its NIC to that subnet, and add the NIC to the backend pool (C). Finally configure the health probe and load-balancing rule and verify traffic reaches the VM (D).

A common error is creating load-balancing rules before any backend members or a health probe exist, which leaves traffic with nowhere healthy to go.
references: AZ-104: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources — load balancing a VM

questions.stem: VNet-Hub (10.0.0.0/16) is peered to VNet-Spoke1 (10.1.0.0/16) and VNet-Spoke2 (10.2.0.0/16). Spoke1 VMs cannot reach Spoke2 VMs. Peering between the spokes does not exist. Which networking concept explains this, and what is the simplest fix to enable spoke-to-spoke traffic through the hub?

options.text: VNet peering is transitive by default, so the issue must be an NSG; no routing change is needed
VNet peering is non-transitive; deploy a gateway/NVA in the hub and use user-defined routes (and enable gateway transit/forwarding) so spokes route to each other via the hub
Spokes can never communicate; you must merge them into one VNet
Enable global peering between the hub and each spoke to make peering transitive

questions.explanation:
**Correct (B):** VNet peering is not transitive — traffic does not automatically flow Spoke1 to Spoke2 through the hub just because both peer with the hub. The hub-and-spoke fix is to route spoke-to-spoke traffic through a gateway or NVA in the hub using user-defined routes (with appropriate forwarding/gateway transit), so the hub relays the traffic.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **A** Peering is non-transitive, so this is a routing problem, not merely an NSG rule.
- **C** Spokes can communicate via the hub with routing/an appliance; merging VNets is unnecessary.
- **D** Global peering connects VNets across regions but is still non-transitive; it does not make traffic flow through the hub.
references: AZ-104: Implement and manage virtual networking — peering and transitivity

questions.stem: A subnet hosts application VMs that must reach Azure Storage and Azure SQL over the Microsoft backbone, and you also want the storage account to accept traffic only from this subnet using the service's public endpoint. Which feature should you enable on the subnet?

options.text: A NAT gateway on the subnet
A private endpoint in a different subnet
A service endpoint for Microsoft.Storage (and Microsoft.Sql) on the subnet
A user-defined route to 0.0.0.0/0

questions.explanation:
**Correct (C):** A service endpoint extends the subnet's identity to the Azure service over the backbone and lets you lock the storage account firewall to accept traffic only from that subnet (using the service's public endpoint). Enabling Microsoft.Storage and Microsoft.Sql endpoints on the subnet matches the requirement exactly.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **A** A NAT gateway provides outbound internet SNAT; it does not restrict a storage account to a subnet.
- **B** A private endpoint gives the service a private IP in your VNet — a valid alternative pattern, but it does not use the service's public endpoint as the question specifies, and it is a different feature than the subnet service endpoint described.
- **D** A default route changes egress routing and does not implement service-endpoint-based access control.
references: AZ-104: Implement and manage virtual networking — service endpoints

questions.stem: A subnet NSG has these inbound rules plus the defaults: priority 200 Allow TCP 443 from Internet; priority 300 Deny TCP 443 from 203.0.113.10/32. A request arrives on TCP 443 from 203.0.113.10. What happens and why?

options.text: Allowed, because NSG rules are processed by priority and the Allow at 200 matches first
Denied, because the more specific /32 deny rule takes precedence over the broader allow
Denied, because the default DenyAllInbound rule always wins
Allowed, because deny rules are ignored when an allow rule for the same port exists

questions.explanation:
**Correct (A):** NSG rules are evaluated strictly in priority order (lower number first), and the first matching rule wins. The Allow at priority 200 matches the TCP 443 request before the Deny at 300 is ever considered, so the traffic is allowed. Specificity does not matter — only priority.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **B** NSGs do not use longest-prefix/specificity; they use priority order, so the /32 deny at 300 never gets evaluated.
- **C** The default DenyAllInbound has a very high priority number (lowest precedence) and only applies if no earlier rule matches.
- **D** Deny rules are not generally ignored; here it is simply that the allow rule has higher precedence by priority.
references: AZ-104: Implement and manage virtual networking — NSG rule processing

questions.stem: You must publish a public web application that requires URL path-based routing, host-based routing, TLS termination, and a Web Application Firewall. Which Azure service should you choose?

options.text: Azure Load Balancer (Standard)
Azure Bastion
Azure Traffic Manager
Azure Application Gateway with WAF

questions.explanation:
**Correct (D):** Application Gateway is a Layer-7 load balancer that provides URL path-based and host-based routing and TLS termination, and its WAF SKU adds a Web Application Firewall — exactly the requirements listed.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **A** Azure Load Balancer operates at Layer 4 (TCP/UDP) and has no URL/host routing, TLS termination, or WAF.
- **B** Azure Bastion provides secure RDP/SSH to VMs, not web application delivery.
- **C** Traffic Manager is DNS-based global routing; it does not terminate TLS, do path routing, or provide a WAF.
references: AZ-104: Implement and manage virtual networking — Application Gateway

questions.stem: You are designing private DNS resolution for resources in an Azure virtual network. Which statements about Azure Private DNS zones are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Linking a private DNS zone to a VNet allows resources in that VNet to resolve records in the zone
Private DNS zones are reachable and resolvable from the public internet by default
Enabling auto-registration on a VNet link automatically creates DNS records for VMs deployed in that VNet
A single VNet can have auto-registration enabled for multiple private DNS zones simultaneously
Private DNS zones are commonly used with private endpoints so a service's public FQDN resolves to its private IP

questions.explanation:
**Correct (A, C, E):** A virtual network link makes a private zone's records resolvable from that VNet (A). Auto-registration on the link creates and maintains A records for VMs in the VNet automatically (C). Private DNS zones are a key part of the private endpoint pattern, mapping a service's FQDN to its private IP (E).

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **B** Private DNS zones are private to linked VNets; they are not resolvable from the public internet.
- **D** A VNet can have auto-registration enabled for only one private DNS zone at a time, though it can be linked (without auto-registration) to others.
references: AZ-104: Implement and manage virtual networking — Azure Private DNS

questions.stem: VMs in a subnet have no public IP. They must make outbound calls to internet APIs reliably at scale, and you want to avoid SNAT port exhaustion that can occur with default outbound access or load-balancer outbound rules. What should you deploy?

options.text: An Azure Bastion host in the subnet
A NAT gateway associated with the subnet
A user-defined route sending traffic to the internet next hop
A public IP on each VM's network interface

questions.explanation:
**Correct (B):** A NAT gateway provides scalable, reliable outbound connectivity for a subnet and dramatically reduces SNAT port exhaustion by managing large pools of SNAT ports, all without assigning public IPs to the VMs.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **A** Bastion is for inbound management (RDP/SSH) access, not outbound internet egress for workloads.
- **C** A UDR can direct traffic but does not by itself provide scalable SNAT; it does not solve port exhaustion.
- **D** Putting public IPs on every VM increases exposure and management overhead and is the opposite of the private, NAT-based approach desired.
references: AZ-104: Implement and manage virtual networking — NAT gateway

questions.stem: You add a user-defined route table to a subnet with a route 0.0.0.0/0 -> next hop type Virtual Appliance at 10.0.100.4, to force all egress through a firewall NVA. The NVA VM drops the traffic. The NVA's NIC is configured correctly. What setting is most likely missing that prevents the NVA from forwarding traffic?

options.text: The route table is not associated with the NVA's own subnet
The subnet is missing a service endpoint for Microsoft.Network
IP forwarding is not enabled on the NVA's network interface
The NVA needs a public IP address to forward private traffic

questions.explanation:
**Correct (C):** For a VM to act as a router/NVA and forward packets that are not addressed to itself, IP forwarding must be enabled on its network interface (and the OS must also be configured to forward). Without it, Azure drops the forwarded packets.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **A** The UDR must be on the source subnet (which it is); associating it with the NVA's own subnet is not what enables forwarding and could even cause a routing loop.
- **B** Service endpoints relate to reaching Azure PaaS services, not NVA packet forwarding.
- **D** Forwarding private/egress traffic does not require a public IP on the NVA; IP forwarding on the NIC is the missing piece.
references: AZ-104: Implement and manage virtual networking — UDR and NVAs

questions.stem: You need to give a public DNS name 'shop.contoso.com' to point directly to an IPv4 address that you own and that does not change. The zone 'contoso.com' is hosted in Azure DNS. Which record type should you create?

options.text: An A record
A CNAME record
An MX record
A TXT record

questions.explanation:
**Correct (A):** An A record maps a hostname directly to an IPv4 address, which is exactly what is needed for shop.contoso.com to resolve to your fixed IPv4 address.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **B** A CNAME points a name to another name (alias), not directly to an IP address.
- **C** An MX record specifies mail exchangers for a domain, unrelated to mapping a host to an IP.
- **D** A TXT record holds arbitrary text (e.g., SPF, verification), not an address mapping.
references: AZ-104: Implement and manage virtual networking — Azure DNS records

questions.stem: Two subnets in the same VNet, 'web' and 'data', each have an NSG. You want to allow only the web tier to reach the data tier on TCP 1433, while keeping rules manageable as VMs are added and removed. Which approach is best?

options.text: Hard-code each web VM's private IP in the data NSG allow rule
Open TCP 1433 from any source on the data NSG
Disable the NSG on the data subnet and rely on the VNet boundary
Place web VMs' NICs in an Application Security Group and write the data NSG rule to allow that ASG as source on TCP 1433

questions.explanation:
**Correct (D):** Application Security Groups let you group VM NICs logically (for example, all web servers) and reference that group as the source in an NSG rule. As VMs are added or removed you just change ASG membership, and the NSG rule referencing the ASG stays the same — manageable and least-privilege.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **A** Hard-coding IPs is brittle and high-maintenance as VMs change.
- **B** Allowing 1433 from any source over-exposes the database tier, violating least privilege.
- **C** Disabling the data NSG removes protection entirely; the VNet boundary does not restrict intra-VNet traffic between subnets.
references: AZ-104: Implement and manage virtual networking — Application Security Groups

questions.stem: You must collect guest-OS performance counters and Syslog/Windows event logs from many Azure VMs into a Log Analytics workspace, using the current recommended agent and configuration approach. Which combination should you use?

options.text: Install the legacy Log Analytics agent (MMA) and configure data sources in the workspace
Deploy the Azure Monitor Agent (AMA) and define what to collect with a Data Collection Rule (DCR)
Enable boot diagnostics on each VM
Turn on Azure Activity log export to the workspace

questions.explanation:
**Correct (B):** The Azure Monitor Agent is the current, recommended agent for collecting guest telemetry, and what it collects (perf counters, Syslog, Windows events) is defined declaratively in Data Collection Rules that target the VMs and send data to the workspace.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **A** The Log Analytics agent (MMA/OMS) is the legacy approach being retired in favor of AMA.
- **C** Boot diagnostics captures console/screenshot output for troubleshooting boot issues, not ongoing perf/log collection.
- **D** The Activity log records control-plane operations on resources, not guest-OS performance counters or Syslog.
references: AZ-104: Monitor and maintain Azure resources — Azure Monitor Agent and DCR

questions.stem: You configure a metric alert for high CPU and want the same notification and remediation actions (email the team, trigger a Logic App) reused by several alerts without redefining them each time. Which Azure Monitor component should you create?

options.text: An alert processing rule suppression
A diagnostic setting
An action group
A Log Analytics saved search

questions.explanation:
**Correct (C):** An action group is a reusable collection of notification and action targets (email, SMS, webhook, Logic App, Function, etc.). You attach the same action group to multiple alert rules, so you define the actions once and reuse them.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **A** Alert processing (action) rules can suppress or modify notifications but are not the reusable container of the notification targets themselves.
- **B** A diagnostic setting routes resource logs/metrics to destinations; it does not define alert notifications/actions.
- **D** A saved search stores a query in Log Analytics; it does not define alert actions.
references: AZ-104: Monitor and maintain Azure resources — action groups

questions.stem: You need to verify whether outbound traffic from a specific VM to a destination IP on TCP 443 is allowed or blocked by the effective NSG rules, and to identify exactly which rule is responsible. Which Network Watcher capability should you use?

options.text: IP flow verify
Connection Monitor
NSG flow logs
Next hop

questions.explanation:
**Correct (A):** IP flow verify checks whether a packet is allowed or denied to/from a VM for a given direction, protocol, port, and remote IP, and it returns the name of the NSG rule that made the decision — exactly the diagnostic described.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **B** Connection Monitor measures ongoing reachability/latency between endpoints over time, not a single allow/deny rule decision.
- **C** NSG flow logs record traffic for later analysis but do not interactively tell you, for one flow, which rule allows or denies it on demand.
- **D** Next hop tells you the routing next hop for a destination, not the NSG allow/deny decision.
references: AZ-104: Monitor and maintain Azure resources — Network Watcher IP flow verify

questions.stem: You protect Azure VMs with Azure Backup using a Recovery Services vault. Which statements about Azure Backup for VMs are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Azure Backup for VMs requires you to manually script VSS snapshots before each backup
A backup policy defines the schedule and retention for recovery points
Backup data for a VM can only be restored to the exact same VM it was taken from
You can restore an entire VM, or restore individual files/folders by mounting the recovery point
Soft delete in the Recovery Services vault retains deleted backup data for a period so it can be recovered

questions.explanation:
**Correct (B, D, E):** A backup policy sets the backup schedule and how long recovery points are kept (B). Restores can be full-VM or file-level by mounting the recovery point as a drive (D). Vault soft delete keeps deleted backups for a retention window so accidental or malicious deletion can be reversed (E).

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **A** Azure Backup coordinates application-consistent snapshots (including VSS on Windows) automatically; you do not hand-script VSS per backup.
- **C** You can restore to a new VM or restore disks and attach them elsewhere; restore is not limited to the original VM.
references: AZ-104: Monitor and maintain Azure resources — Azure Backup for VMs

questions.stem: You use Azure Site Recovery to replicate production VMs from East US to West US. Before declaring DR readiness, you must confirm the VMs boot and apps work in West US without affecting ongoing replication or the production workload. What should you perform?

options.text: A planned failover to West US
Disable replication and recreate the VMs manually in West US
An unplanned failover and then fail back
A test failover into an isolated network in West US

questions.explanation:
**Correct (D):** A test failover spins up the replicated VMs in an isolated test network in the target region so you can validate boot and application behavior, all without impacting the source production VMs or the ongoing replication. You then clean up the test.

**Why the others are wrong:**
- **A** A planned failover actually moves the workload to the target region (used for known events), disrupting production rather than just testing.
- **B** Disabling replication and manually recreating VMs defeats the purpose of ASR and removes your DR protection.
- **C** An unplanned failover is for real disasters and shifts the live workload; failing back adds further disruption — not a non-impacting test.
references: AZ-104: Monitor and maintain Azure resources — Azure Site Recovery test failover

questions.stem: Auditors require that subscription-level Activity Log records (who created, updated, or deleted resources) be retained and queryable for two years. By default Azure keeps Activity Log entries for only 90 days. What should you configure to meet the requirement?

options.text: Increase the Activity Log retention slider in the subscription's Activity Log blade to 730 days
Create a diagnostic setting on the Activity Log that exports the entries to a Log Analytics workspace with 730-day retention
Enable a Recovery Services vault and add the Activity Log as a backup item
Turn on boot diagnostics so the events are written to a managed storage account

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** The Activity Log is kept only 90 days, so to retain it longer you create a diagnostic setting that exports entries to a Log Analytics workspace and set the workspace retention as needed. Why the others are wrong: **A** no retention slider extends the Activity Log past 90 days; **C** Recovery Services vaults back up VMs and files, not platform logs; **D** boot diagnostics captures VM serial logs and screenshots, not the Activity Log.
references: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/credentials/certifications/resources/study-guides/az-104

questions.stem: In Log Analytics you must produce a count of Heartbeat records per computer grouped into 1-hour buckets so you can spot VMs that stopped reporting. Which Kusto Query Language (KQL) construct produces that hourly, per-computer aggregation?

options.text: Heartbeat | where TimeGenerated > ago(1h) | take 100
Heartbeat | sort by TimeGenerated desc | project Computer, TimeGenerated
Heartbeat | summarize count() by Computer, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
Heartbeat | distinct Computer | count

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** summarize applies an aggregation (count()) grouped by the by columns, and bin(TimeGenerated, 1h) rounds timestamps into one-hour buckets, giving a per-computer hourly count. Why the others are wrong: **A** where/take just filters and samples rows without aggregating; **B** sort/project only orders and selects columns; **D** distinct + count yields a single total of unique computers, not an hourly time series.
references: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/credentials/certifications/resources/study-guides/az-104
