questions.stem: Your security team runs a third-party SIEM and wants Azure platform (resource) logs streamed to it in near real time for ingestion. You are configuring a diagnostic setting on the resources. Which destination should you select so the SIEM can consume the streamed events?

options.text: An Azure Storage account
A Log Analytics workspace
A Recovery Services vault
An Azure Event Hubs namespace

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** Diagnostic settings stream logs to an Event Hubs namespace, the standard integration point for forwarding Azure platform logs to third-party SIEM tools in near real time. Why the others are wrong: **A** Storage is for cheap archival, not real-time streaming; **B** a Log Analytics workspace is for KQL analysis in Azure, not feeding an external SIEM stream; **C** a Recovery Services vault is a backup target, not a diagnostic-setting destination.
references: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/credentials/certifications/resources/study-guides/az-104

questions.stem: You are planning diagnostic settings for an Azure resource and need to send its resource logs to two separate Log Analytics workspaces as well as to a Storage account. Which two statements about Azure Monitor diagnostic settings are correct? (Select two.)

options.text: A single diagnostic setting can list two Log Analytics workspaces as destinations at the same time
A single diagnostic setting can include at most one of each destination type (one workspace, one Storage account, one Event Hubs)
A resource can have only one diagnostic setting total
To send the same logs to two Log Analytics workspaces you must create two separate diagnostic settings

questions.explanation: **Correct (B, D):** A diagnostic setting can define no more than one of each destination type, so reaching two workspaces requires a second diagnostic setting; a resource can have several settings (up to five). Why the others are wrong: **A** one setting cannot target two workspaces simultaneously; **C** a resource is not limited to a single diagnostic setting, so this is false.
references: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/credentials/certifications/resources/study-guides/az-104

questions.stem: You must continuously measure reachability, latency, and packet loss between an Azure VM and an on-premises server at regular intervals, record the results over time, and raise alerts when connectivity degrades. Which Network Watcher capability should you use?

options.text: Connection monitor
Connection troubleshoot
IP flow verify
Next hop

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Connection monitor gives end-to-end, continuous monitoring of Azure and hybrid endpoints at set intervals, tracking reachability and latency over time with metrics and alerts. Why the others are wrong: **B** connection troubleshoot tests connectivity only at a point in time, not continuously; **C** IP flow verify checks NSG allow/deny, not latency over time; **D** next hop diagnoses routing, not ongoing connectivity health.
references: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/credentials/certifications/resources/study-guides/az-104

questions.stem: For a security investigation you must capture a record of all IP traffic flowing through a network security group, persist that data, and then visualize traffic patterns and top talkers. Which Network Watcher feature provides the rich visualization layer over this captured flow data?

options.text: IP flow verify
Packet capture
Traffic analytics (over flow logs)
Effective security rules

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Flow logs record IP traffic through an NSG or VNet and store it in Azure Storage; Traffic analytics then visualizes that flow log data, including top talkers and patterns. Why the others are wrong: **A** IP flow verify tests one allow/deny decision, it does not log or visualize traffic; **B** packet capture grabs raw packets for a VM, not aggregated analytics; **D** effective security rules lists rules on a NIC, not traffic flows.
references: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/credentials/certifications/resources/study-guides/az-104

questions.stem: Soft delete is enabled on your Recovery Services vault. An administrator deletes the backup of a critical VM. You did not change the soft-delete retention. For how long does Azure keep the deleted backup data in a recoverable, no-extra-charge state by default before it is permanently removed?

options.text: 7 days
14 days
30 days
90 days

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** With soft delete the default retention is 14 days, during which the deleted backup data is recoverable at no additional cost; the duration can be raised (up to 180 days), but beyond 14 days incurs charges. Why the others are wrong: **A** 7 days is not the soft-delete default; **C** 30 days is a common backup retention value but not the soft-delete default; **D** 90 days is the Activity Log default, not soft delete.
references: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/credentials/certifications/resources/study-guides/az-104

questions.stem: A user accidentally deleted a few files from an Azure VM that is protected by Azure Backup. You must recover only those individual files from last night's recovery point without restoring the entire VM or its disks. What is the correct approach?

options.text: Use file recovery (item-level recovery): download and run the vault-provided script that mounts the recovery point as iSCSI disks, then copy the files
Perform a Replace existing restore to overwrite the VM's disks with the recovery point
Create a new VM from the recovery point and copy the files off it
Restore the VM disks to a Storage account and attach them to another VM

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** File recovery (item-level recovery) generates a downloadable script that mounts the chosen recovery point as iSCSI volumes, letting you browse and copy individual files without a full restore. Why the others are wrong: **B** replace existing overwrites all VM disks, far more disruptive than needed; **C** creating a whole new VM is heavyweight for a few files; **D** restoring full disks is a disk-level operation, not item-level recovery.
references: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/credentials/certifications/resources/study-guides/az-104

questions.stem: An Azure VM is unreachable and appears stuck during startup, so you cannot connect over RDP or SSH. You want to view the OS console screen image and serial boot output to diagnose the boot failure. Which VM feature must be enabled to capture this screenshot and serial log?

options.text: Network Watcher connection troubleshoot
Application Insights
Azure Backup instant restore
Boot diagnostics

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** Boot diagnostics captures the VM's serial boot log and a screenshot of the console, which is exactly what you inspect when a VM fails to boot or hangs at startup; it is also a prerequisite for Serial Console. Why the others are wrong: **A** connection troubleshoot tests network connectivity, not OS boot state; **B** Application Insights monitors application telemetry, not VM boot; **C** instant restore recovers backup data and does not show live boot output.
references: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/credentials/certifications/resources/study-guides/az-104

flashcards.front: What is the key difference between Azure RBAC roles and Azure Policy?
flashcards.back: RBAC controls WHO can perform WHICH actions on resources (authorization). Azure Policy controls WHAT configurations resources are allowed to have (compliance/enforcement), e.g. allowed regions or required tags. They are complementary, not interchangeable.

flashcards.front: What are the two types of resource locks and what does each prevent?
flashcards.back: CanNotDelete: resources can be read and modified but not deleted. ReadOnly: resources can be read but not modified or deleted (and ReadOnly blocks operations like listing/rotating storage keys, which are write actions).

flashcards.front: Compare LRS, ZRS, GRS, and RA-GRS for storage redundancy.
flashcards.back: LRS: 3 copies in one datacenter. ZRS: copies across availability zones in one region. GRS: LRS in primary plus async copy to a secondary region (secondary not readable until failover). RA-GRS: GRS plus read access to the secondary region at all times.

flashcards.front: When should you use a SAS token instead of the storage account access key?
flashcards.back: Use a SAS to grant scoped, time-limited, optionally IP/permission-restricted access to specific storage resources without exposing the all-powerful account key. Tie a SAS to a stored access policy so you can revoke it before its expiry.

flashcards.front: What do blob soft delete and blob versioning protect against?
flashcards.back: Soft delete retains deleted blobs (and snapshots) for a retention period so they can be restored. Versioning automatically saves the previous state of a blob whenever it is overwritten or deleted, so you can recover an earlier version.

flashcards.front: Availability set vs availability zone — what does each protect against?
flashcards.back: Availability set: spreads VMs across fault and update domains within a SINGLE datacenter to survive hardware failures and host maintenance. Availability zone: spreads VMs across physically separate datacenters in a region to survive an entire datacenter failure (higher SLA).

flashcards.front: Container Instances vs Container Apps vs AKS — when to use each?
flashcards.back: ACI: simplest, single short-lived containers, per-second billing, no orchestration. Container Apps: serverless containers with event/HTTP autoscaling and scale-to-zero, no cluster management. AKS: full managed Kubernetes for complex, large-scale orchestration where you control node pools.

flashcards.front: Service endpoint vs private endpoint for accessing Azure PaaS services.
flashcards.back: Service endpoint: extends your VNet identity to the PaaS service over the Microsoft backbone, but the service is still reached via its public endpoint. Private endpoint (Private Link): gives the PaaS resource a private IP inside your subnet so it is reachable privately and the public endpoint can be disabled.

flashcards.front: For inbound traffic, how are a subnet NSG and a NIC NSG evaluated together?
flashcards.back: Both apply. Inbound traffic is checked against the subnet NSG first, then the NIC NSG; the traffic must be allowed by BOTH to reach the VM. A deny at either layer blocks it. (Outbound is evaluated NIC NSG first, then subnet NSG.)

flashcards.front: Azure Backup vs Azure Site Recovery — what is each for?
flashcards.back: Azure Backup: scheduled point-in-time backups with retention, stored in a Recovery Services vault, for restoring data/VMs. Azure Site Recovery: continuous replication of VMs to a secondary region for disaster recovery and failover (low RPO). They solve different problems and are often used together.
